paragraphs.text: Or “Jacob.” The James who wrote this letter is evidently the half brother of Jesus Christ. (Mt 13:55 and study note; Mr 6:3; Ga 1:19 and study note) During Christ’s ministry on earth, James did not put faith in his older brother, but he became a faithful disciple shortly after Jesus’ death and resurrection. (Joh 7:3-5; Ac 1:14 and study note; 1Co 15:7) James served as a respected overseer in the Christian congregation in Jerusalem. (Ga 2:9; see study notes on Ac 12:17; 15:13.) In the Christian Greek Scriptures, four people were named James (Greek, I·aʹko·bos). This was a common name among Jews, apparently because it was the Greek equivalent of Jacob, the name of the patriarch (spelled I·a·kobʹ in the Septuagint). However, Bible writers used the Greek spelling for James while retaining the Septuagint spelling for Jacob the patriarch and for Jacob the father of Joseph the husband of Mary. (Mt 1:2, 15, 16; Lu 1:33; Joh 4:5) Paul indicates that at least some of Jesus’ brothers were married.—1Co 9:5.

paragraphs.lemma: a slave of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ
paragraphs.text: In his opening greeting, James modestly avoids mentioning that he is related to the Lord Jesus Christ. Instead, James calls himself “a slave of God and of . . . Jesus Christ,” indicating his submission to them. James’ brother Jude, as well as the apostles Paul and Peter, used similar greetings in their letters. (Jude 1 and study note; Ro 1:1 and study note; 2Pe 1:1) And throughout his letter, James addresses his readers as “brothers,” “my brothers,” or “my beloved brothers,” showing his humility, affection, and empathy for them. (Jas 1:2, 16, 19; 2:1, 5, 14; 3:1, 10, 12; 4:11; 5:7, 9, 10, 12, 19) No doubt, his humble attitude made it easier for the recipients of the letter to accept his advice and strong counsel.

paragraphs.lemma: the 12 tribes that are scattered about
paragraphs.text: The tribes addressed here are not fleshly Israelites but the spirit-anointed “heirs of the Kingdom”—the spiritual “Israel of God.” (Jas 2:1, 5; Ga 6:15, 16 and study note) James’ use of this expression reflects Jehovah’s viewpoint. This new nation had replaced the 12 tribes of fleshly Israel as His chosen people. (Compare Re 7:4-8; 21:12.) Those belonging to the worldwide congregation of anointed Christians were “scattered about” (lit., “in the dispersion”) in the sense that they lived throughout the Greco-Roman world.—1Pe 1:1; compare study note on Joh 7:35.
See study note on Ac 15:23.

Although trials are not inherently joyous experiences, James reminds his readers that Christians can choose how to “consider,” or view, such challenges. If they choose to see their trials as opportunities to test and strengthen their faith, the end result is “all joy,” or “nothing but joy.” (See also Mt 5:11, 12; Ro 5:3-5.) That counsel applies to how we view a wide variety of hardships.

This expression may suggest an unexpected and unwelcome encounter, as when a man “fell victim” to robbers. (See Lu 10:30, where the same Greek verb is used.) James thus implies that some trials may arise abruptly and unexpectedly. (Compare Ec 9:11.) In this letter, he discusses a variety of trials, such as those resulting from persecution, the behavior of fellow believers, and a Christian’s own imperfections.—Jas 1:14; 2:1, 6, 7; 4:1, 2, 11.

The Greek word here rendered “various” may also mean “diversified” or “many-colored”—as in the plumage of a colorful bird. At 1Pe 4:10, a form of the same word is applied to the undeserved kindness of God. (See study note on 1Pe 4:10.) While James says that trials may come in a wide variety of “colors,” Peter assures Christians that God’s undeserved kindness is likewise expressed in many “colors.” Thus, God is in a sense able to help his servants endure any trial that they may face, providing just the right expression of undeserved kindness to help them endure.—Ps 34:19.

The expression “tested quality” translates a Greek word that refers to testing something to prove whether it is genuine. It was also used regarding the process of refining gold or silver by fire. Only after being refined would such precious metals prove to be truly genuine and pure. This word was used twice in the Greek Septuagint translation to refer to the refining process or to a refining pot. (Ps 12:6 [11:7, LXX]; Pr 27:21) The apostle Peter used it in a similar way regarding faith. (1Pe 1:7) Here James shows that Christians who allow their trials to refine their faith, proving it genuine, can develop another precious quality—endurance.

When under trial, Christians might wish that the hardships they face would end quickly. They might even be tempted to violate Jehovah’s principles in order to avoid a trial. James reminds Christians that undergoing such trials can help to build qualities that are precious to God, especially endurance. (See study note on Ro 5:3.) Speaking about “endurance” as used in the Scriptures, one reference work describes it as “the spirit which can bear things, not simply with resignation, but with blazing hope.” The same work adds: “It is the quality which keeps a man on his feet with his face to the wind. It is the virtue which can transmute the hardest trial into glory because beyond the pain it sees the goal.”

let . . . complete its work, so that you may be complete: The Greek word rendered “complete” is used twice in this verse and can convey a broad range of meanings. In the first occurrence, it conveys the idea “let endurance finish its work.” In the second occurrence, it could be translated “so that you may be full-grown [mature; perfect].” (Compare Mt 5:48 and study note; Eph 4:13; Php 3:15.) In the Septuagint, the same word is used to convey the meaning of “faultless” (Ge 6:9) or “blameless” (2Sa 22:26). It can also describe a heart that is “complete” in its devotion to Jehovah.—1Ki 8:61 and ftn.

The single Greek term rendered “sound in all respects” may also convey the meaning of “whole” or “blameless.” By combining the terms “complete and sound in all respects,” James expresses confidence that humans—despite being imperfect—can meet a lofty standard of faithfulness. James conveys an idea similar to the concept of integrity mentioned in the Hebrew Scriptures, that is, whole, or complete, devotion to Jehovah. (Jos 24:14 and ftn.; Job 27:5; Ps 26:1; 101:2 and ftn.) James thus emphasizes that endurance can help make an imperfect human complete in the sense of remaining faithful to Jehovah and keeping integrity even under trial.—See also Job 1:1, 8; 2:3.

paragraphs.lemma: if any one of you is lacking in wisdom
paragraphs.text: James here refers to wisdom from Jehovah, the only wisdom that can help a Christian to remain faithful in times of trial. (Compare Pr 2:1, 2, 5, 6; 21:30.) James’ encouragement to keep asking God echoes Jesus’ counsel to “keep on asking.” (Mt 7:7 and study note, 8; Lu 11:9, 10) By persisting in prayer, Christians would show how strongly they desire to make decisions that Jehovah can bless. Also, by continuing to seek God’s guidance, they would allow holy spirit to help them see how to apply God’s wisdom to their situation.—Lu 11:13; Joh 14:26.

paragraphs.lemma: he gives generously to all and without reproaching
paragraphs.text: James gives his readers three reasons to be confident when asking Jehovah for wisdom: First, “he gives generously.” God stands ready to provide more than enough wisdom, without reservation. (Pr 2:6; Ro 11:33; compare 1Ki 4:29.) Second, as the impartial God, he responds “to all” who keep on requesting and seeking wisdom from him. (Pr 2:3-5; Mt 7:7; Ac 10:34) Third, God gives “without reproaching” (or, “without finding fault”), that is, kindly, without scolding or embarrassing the one asking. James here describes not only God’s promise to provide wisdom but also His disposition. Jehovah never becomes weary of repeated prayers for wisdom on the part of his worshippers.—Lu 18:1-8.

The Greek verb rendered “doubting” and “doubts” in this verse conveys the idea of being uncertain, divided in one’s mind, indecisive. The same verb is rendered “waver” at Ro 4:20. (See study note.) In the Christian Greek Scriptures, doubt is contrasted with faith in various contexts. Jesus showed that doubt can involve weakness of faith when he told Peter: “You with little faith, why did you give way to doubt?” (Mt 14:31; see study note on Mt 17:20.) James here discusses the danger of doubting whether God will answer a Christian’s sincere prayers for wisdom. Instead of giving in to doubts, a Christian should keep asking in faith, that is, in full confidence that God will respond.—See study note on Mt 7:7; compare study note on Jude 22.

paragraphs.lemma: like a wave of the sea
paragraphs.text: James likens a person who lacks faith—a person who has doubts when he prays to God—to restless and unpredictable waves that surge in every direction as they are “driven by the wind.” Such waves would have been a familiar sight to James, who grew up in Nazareth, not far from both the Sea of Galilee and the Mediterranean Sea. (Regarding James’ use of illustrations, see “Introduction to James.”) A doubter is swayed by every “wind”—every outside influence, every fear, every pressure of circumstances. (Jas 1:8; compare Eph 4:14.) James exhorts such a person to pray to Jehovah with confidence, assured that He hears his petitions and answers them in His own time and way.—Jas 1:5; 1Jo 5:14, 15.

The Scriptures leave no doubt that Jehovah is the Source of true wisdom and that he gives it generously to those who humbly seek it from him. (Ex 31:2, 3; 1Ki 3:7-12; 4:29, 30; Pr 2:6; Mt 7:11; Lu 11:13; Jas 1:5, 6) However, a person who doubts Jehovah’s generosity and his willingness to come to the aid of his servants cannot rightly expect to receive wisdom or guidance from him. The apostle Paul made a similar point by saying: “Whoever approaches God must believe that he is and that he becomes the rewarder of those earnestly seeking him.”—Heb 11:6 and study note; for the use of the divine name at Jas 1:7, see App. C3 introduction; Jas 1:7.

This phrase describes a man given to doubting, an indication that he fails to put his trust in God. The Greek word James uses literally means “two-souled.” It may convey the idea of being double-minded, trying to go in two directions at once. A man like that is torn between devotion to God and the pull of his own selfish heart. (Compare Pr 28:26; Jer 17:9; Mt 6:24.) He might even hesitate to take matters to God in prayer. James adds that such a man is unsteady in all his ways, that is, in all his actions. The Greek term for “unsteady” is used in the Septuagint at Isa 54:11 to render a Hebrew word for “storm-tossed.” By using this term, James may be continuing the maritime illustration he started at Jas 1:6.—See study notes on Jas 1:6; 4:8.

paragraphs.lemma: let the lowly brother rejoice over his exaltation
paragraphs.text: Many Christians in the first century were “lowly” in the sense that they were not wealthy; nor did they occupy an important position in society. (1Co 1:26-28) Yet, they could “rejoice” (lit., “boast”) over their “exaltation,” that is, over the fact that they had God’s favor and could rightly look forward to their reward as “heirs of the Kingdom.”—Jas 2:5.

paragraphs.lemma: and the rich one over his humiliation
paragraphs.text: In this context, James urges wealthy Christians to remember that material possessions or social status should not be the source of their joy. Such things are fragile and temporary, and those pursuing them are like a flower of the field, passing away after only a brief span of life. (Jas 1:11 and study note) For those who were rich, becoming Christians may have led to humiliation from a worldly standpoint because such a change often involved the loss of wealth and prestige. (Php 3:8; Heb 10:34 and study note) Yet, no matter what sacrifices those Christians had to make, they could rejoice in knowing that they were pleasing God and would enjoy a rich heavenly reward.—Ro 8:17.

Or “his lowliness”; “his being made lowly (humble).” Greek words related to the word rendered “humiliation” are translated “lowly” in the preceding verse and “humble yourselves” at Jas 4:10. Therefore, James was not using the term “humiliation” to imply that wealthy Christians should feel ashamed of having material assets. Rather, such Christians should rejoice because they had come to view themselves and their possessions correctly. (Mt 13:22; compare Lu 12:21.) In fact, all in the congregation could rejoice in cultivating humility, or lowliness of mind, knowing that Jehovah “gives undeserved kindness to the humble ones.”—Jas 4:6 and study note; 1Pe 5:5 and study note.

paragraphs.lemma: the rich man will fade away
paragraphs.text: James may here be alluding to the word picture at Isa 40:6-8. He uses the withering of a plant and its flower to highlight how fragile and temporary life is—even for the rich. (See also Job 14:1, 2.) Regarding this botanical illustration, one reference work states: “The image of the quickly fading flower would have been a familiar one for Middle Eastern readers who annually saw the early spring flowers wither suddenly under the sun’s merciless heat.” The Greek term here rendered scorching heat was used in the Septuagint to refer to the hot desert wind that came from S and E. (Ho 13:15; compare Lu 12:55.) Just as a plant that appears to be flourishing can quickly and unexpectedly die, a person can lose his life at any time, regardless of how wealthy he may be. Jesus likewise warned that those who pursue riches but ignore God would not enjoy their possessions for long. (Lu 12:16-21) Ultimately, they would lose out on the prospect of gaining “the real life.”—1Ti 6:17-19; compare Ec 5:10.

The Christian Greek Scriptures contain several statements on what makes a person happy. (See study notes on Mt 5:3; Ro 4:7.) Here James shows that if a Christian “keeps on enduring trial,” he can be happy because he will gain God’s approval and receive “the crown of life.”—See also study note on Jas 5:11; compare Ro 5:3-5.

paragraphs.lemma: the man who keeps on enduring trial
paragraphs.text: Jehovah does not shield his servants from all trials that are common to human life. Rather, God allows his people to face such trials for several important reasons. For example, God lets them demonstrate their faith and their love for him despite trials. When suffering for righteousness’ sake, they have an opportunity to answer Satan’s challenge that humans serve God for selfish reasons only and not out of love for Him. (Job 1:9-11; Pr 27:11) Jehovah is keenly interested in their well-being throughout such trials and is delighted to see them benefit from the training and refinement that may result from such hardships. (See study notes on Heb 12:5, 7; compare Ps 105:17-22.) Jehovah never abandons his servants in times of trial; rather, he draws closer to them. (Ps 145:18, 19; 1Co 10:13; Heb 13:5) For such reasons, Christians who faithfully endure trials can rightly be called “happy.”—Compare study notes on Jas 1:2.

In verses 3 and 4, James identified the present benefits of endurance when Christians “meet with” various trials. (Jas 1:2) Then here in verse 12, he points out the final outcome—the reward of everlasting life—for the Christian who “keeps on” enduring trials faithfully. (2Ti 4:8; 1Pe 5:4; Re 2:10; see Media Gallery, “A Crown That Can Perish.”) While this letter was primarily addressed to Christians with a heavenly hope, James here states a general principle that would apply to all of God’s servants.

The Bible contains many promises that Jehovah God has made to his servants. (Some examples are Ge 18:19; Jos 23:14; Ac 2:39; 13:32; 26:6; Ro 4:16, 20, 21; Eph 6:2; Tit 1:2; Heb 6:13; Jas 2:5.) It is worth noting, though, that in ancient non-Biblical Greek literature, it was very rare to read about a god who made promises to humans. (See study note on Heb 4:1.) Thus Jehovah stands out as different from how pagan gods were described—he has obligated himself to reward his faithful servants. The record of his dealings shows that his servants can, in turn, fully trust that he will faithfully fulfill all his promises.—Heb 6:17, 18; 10:23; 11:6, 13; for the use of the divine name here, see App. C3 introduction; Jas 1:12.

In this context, the original-language expression conveys the idea of continuous, or enduring, love for Jehovah. When God’s servants face trials or temptations, such love would help them to see how to act so as to please him; it thus motivates them to remain steadfast.—Jas 5:11; 1Jo 5:3.

Six times in verses 12-14, James uses forms of the same Greek root word (pei·raʹzo) or words related to it, and they are rendered “trial,” “under trial,” “being tried,” “cannot be tried,” “try,” and “is tried.” This root word is broad in meaning and may convey the idea of any trial or test, including those that God may allow to come upon his servants. (Jas 1:12 and study note; see also study note on Heb 2:18.) However, the same word may also refer to a temptation, that is, a trial that may lead a servant of God to behave improperly. That is how the term is used in verses 13 and 14.

paragraphs.lemma: let no one say: “I am being tried by God”
paragraphs.text: James here refers to being tempted to do what is bad. He does not want Christians who are undergoing such trials or temptations to think that Jehovah would ever entice a Christian to sin. (Job 34:10, 12; Jas 1:14 and study note) It would be a mistake to blame God for the temptation.—Pr 19:3.

paragraphs.lemma: For with evil things God cannot be tried
paragraphs.text: This phrase could also be rendered: “For with evil things God cannot be tempted.” Therefore, one idea expressed here is that Jehovah cannot be tried, tested, or tempted to act wickedly; nothing will ever make him feel inclined to do something evil. (De 32:4; Hab 1:13) James’ wording also shows that God’s purpose never changed as a result of the evil that Satan caused by rebelling. (Jas 1:17) James’ statement harmonizes with other Scriptural assurances about the unchangeableness of Jehovah’s personality—he always acts in a good, holy, and righteous way. (1Sa 2:2; Ps 145:17; Mr 10:18 and study note) According to one scholar, the overall meaning of James’ statement is: “God has nothing to do with evil.”

paragraphs.lemma: nor does he himself try anyone
paragraphs.text: That is, God does not try anyone with evil things or tempt anyone to do wrong. (Mt 6:13 and study note) Jehovah is the supreme example of such qualities as goodness, holiness, and righteousness, so it is unthinkable that he would commit evil deeds to tempt or try his servants. (Job 34:10, 12) It is impossible for Jehovah to sin or to entice others to sin. Rather, it is Satan who is called “the Tempter.” (1Th 3:5 and study note) As “the wicked one” and “the ruler of this world,” he is the ultimate source of all evil.—1Jo 5:19; Joh 12:31 and study note.
Or “is tempted.”—See study notes on Jas 1:13.

This phrase contains two Greek verbs that were derived from the practices of hunting and fishing. The first verb, here rendered “drawn out,” may suggest the way a fish is lured from the safety of its underwater refuge or the way an animal is lured into a trap or snare. (Ec 9:12) The second verb, “enticed,” could literally be rendered, “lured (caught) as by bait.” It may have brought to mind the way a fish or an animal is attracted to a tempting piece of bait, only to be caught by a hidden hook or trapped in a snare. In both cases, it is the creature’s own desire that is the driving force.

The Greek word rendered “desire” can refer both to proper desires (Lu 22:15; 1Th 2:17) and to improper ones (Ro 13:14; Ga 5:16, 24). However, in this context, the word refers to a yearning for what is forbidden or to an excessive craving. James thus warns that Christians who fail to control such desires are sure to be caught sooner or later.—Compare Ge 3:1-6.

paragraphs.lemma: the desire . . . gives birth to sin
paragraphs.text: Here James, like earlier Bible writers, uses the process of conception and childbirth as a metaphor. (Ps 7:14; Isa 59:4) In saying that the desire has become fertile, he uses a Greek word that literally means “has conceived.” Just as conception naturally leads to birth, so nurturing a wrong desire leads to sin. The next step in the progression is when sin has been carried out, or completed. In harmony with the metaphor James uses, the Greek expression for “when it has been carried out” might also be rendered “when it is full-grown.” The overall idea of his metaphor may be as follows: The desire gives birth to sin. Then sin figuratively grows up and brings forth, or gives birth to, its own “offspring,” death. James thus vividly makes the point that a Christian must stop this process at the outset by refusing to dwell on or indulge in wrong desires.—Compare Mt 5:27-30.

After discussing the true source and the consequences of sin, James sounds a warning, using a strong expression also found in Paul’s writings. (1Co 6:9; 15:33; Ga 6:7) He cautions fellow Christians never to conclude that God is the author of their trials or that He is somehow to blame for any sins they commit. (Jas 1:13-15) On the contrary, James reminds them that God is the Source of “every good gift and every perfect present.” (Jas 1:17) James’ warning, although sobering, is motivated by love for his fellow believers. His use of the expression my beloved brothers reveals that he has great affection for them.—See study note on Jas 1:1.

paragraphs.lemma: Every good gift and every perfect present
paragraphs.text: The Greek word for “gift” that James here uses can also refer to the act of giving. In fact, some translations render the first part of the verse “Every good [or “generous”] act of giving.” The synonymous Greek word translated “present” is the same one that Paul uses at Ro 5:16 in referring to God’s “free gift.” Jehovah’s abundant goodness and generosity motivate him to give freely and bountifully to others. (Ps 145:16; Mt 5:45; Ac 17:25) His gifts are always good and promote the welfare and happiness of the recipients. (Ac 14:17; 1Ti 6:17) In addition, his presents are “perfect,” that is, they lack nothing; each gift is fully suited to provide what is needed in each situation.—2Co 9:8; Php 4:19; 2Ti 3:17.

paragraphs.lemma: the Father of the celestial lights
paragraphs.text: Jehovah is the Father, or Creator, of the sun, moon, and stars, which appear in the sky and shed or reflect light for those who live on earth. (Ge 1:3, 4, 14-18; Ps 136:7-9; Jer 31:35) These celestial, or heavenly, lights are an essential part of creation, and observing them fills humans with awe. (Ps 8:3, 4) Jehovah is also the Source of spiritual enlightenment. His thoughts, found in the inspired Scriptures, enlighten those who choose to be guided by them. (Ps 43:3; 119:105; Pr 6:23; Isa 51:4; 1Jo 1:5 and study note) Thus, light—physical and spiritual—is among the good and perfect presents that come from Jehovah.—Ps 36:9; compare 2Co 4:6 and study notes.

paragraphs.lemma: who does not vary or change like the shifting shadows
paragraphs.text: Here James contrasts the steadfastness of God, the Creator, with the changeableness of creation. He notes that shadows keep changing, shifting throughout the day. They do so because the sun’s position in the sky keeps changing. Jehovah is sometimes likened to a sun because he is the Source of light. (1Jo 1:5; compare Ps 84:11.) Unlike the shifting shadows caused by sunlight, though, God is constant. He rightly says: “I am Jehovah; I do not change.” (Mal 3:6) The Scriptures show that God is good, faithful, righteous, and loving, and he has many other beautiful qualities. (Mt 19:17; 1Jo 1:9; 4:8) Because Jehovah is constant, he shows these qualities continuously, in all circumstances. Therefore, Christians can be certain that he is never the source of any evil things that may befall them. (Jas 1:13) Instead, he is always the Source of “every good gift and every perfect present . . . from above.” The Creator’s steadfastness is referred to numerous times in the Scriptures.—Nu 23:19; De 32:4; Isa 43:10-13; 46:4; Tit 1:1, 2; Heb 6:17, 18.

paragraphs.lemma: It was his will to bring us forth by the word of truth
paragraphs.text: The phrase “to bring us forth” could also be rendered “to give birth to us.” (Compare study note on Jas 1:15.) James here seems to refer to a spiritual birth. When Jehovah anoints humans with his holy spirit, they are born in a special sense, for they now enjoy the hope of spirit life in heaven. (Compare Joh 3:3-6 and study notes on verses 3 and 5.) By using the same Greek word for “bring forth” as in verse 15, James makes the following contrast: “Sin . . . brings forth death,” but God by means of his spirit and “word of truth” brings a new life to the anointed. In this context, “the word of truth” refers to the good news of salvation, the entire body of teachings, that anointed Christians have heard and accepted in faith.—Joh 17:17; Eph 1:13, 14; 1Pe 1:23-25.

paragraphs.lemma: a kind of firstfruits of his creatures
paragraphs.text: James’ readers were familiar with the term “firstfruits,” referring to the first ripe fruits offered to Jehovah at the sanctuary. (Le 23:4-12, 15-20; see Glossary, “Firstfruits.”) The firstfruits of the earliest grain crop, that of barley, were offered on Nisan 16. Correspondingly, Jesus Christ was resurrected to immortal life on that day, becoming the first and primary of the firstfruits to God from among mankind. (For more information about Jesus as the firstfruits, see study note on 1Co 15:20.) His spiritual brothers are, not the primary, but “a kind of” firstfruits, corresponding to the firstfruits of the wheat harvest that were offered later, on the day of Pentecost, Sivan 6. (See App. B15.) They were the first ones to be taken from sinful mankind to become God’s adopted sons, and they would eventually go to heaven to rule with Christ in his Kingdom. (Ro 8:15-17; 1Co 15:23; 1Pe 2:9; Re 14:4; 20:6) Of course, in agriculture, the “firstfruits” constitute only the beginning of the harvest. That expression suggests that a greater ingathering of humans would follow, that is, the ingathering of those who have the hope of living forever on earth and becoming “children of God.”—Ro 8:19-21; see also Mt 5:5.

paragraphs.lemma: Everyone must be quick to listen, slow to speak
paragraphs.text: James here reflects principles from the Hebrew Scriptures about the need to listen carefully and to be cautious when speaking. Failure to listen often leads a person to speak rashly, which may damage his relationships with others and with God. (Le 5:4; Pr 10:19; 15:28; 17:27; 18:13; Heb 2:1; Jas 1:26; 3:1-12) In the following verses (Jas 1:21, 23), James urges his fellow believers to listen carefully to and apply God’s word, or message, in day-to-day life. Since Jehovah is the Source of instruction, God’s people need to read his Word with reverence, eager to understand it correctly. (Job 36:22; Ps 119:102) The Greek word rendered “listen” can carry the sense of obeying, a point that James goes on to develop in verses 22-25. A person who is “slow to speak” would not be quick to argue against divine instruction, even if he did not immediately understand or appreciate it.—1Ti 1:7.

James here echoes a number of Scriptural warnings about the dangers of unbridled anger in imperfect humans. (Ps 37:8; Pr 15:18) Jehovah himself is “slow to anger.” (Ex 34:6; Ps 103:8) And when he does express anger, he does so in a perfect, just way; he is never hasty or harsh. (Compare Jer 30:11.) In contrast, when humans are driven by anger, they are likely to commit impulsive acts. Such deeds often do more harm than good. (Pr 14:29; 25:28) As James goes on to warn in verse 20, “man’s anger does not bring about God’s righteousness.” (Compare study note on Ro 12:19.) The Hebrew Scriptures contain vivid examples of men who were driven by anger to commit terrible sins—or who came dangerously close to doing so.—Ge 34:25, 26; 49:5-7; 1Sa 25:12, 13, 32-34.

The Greek word rendered “filthiness,” according to one reference work, “may literally denote something dirty, or soiled, for example filthy clothes.” (Compare Jas 2:2, where a related word is used in the phrase “a poor man in filthy clothing.”) Figuratively, the word can refer to corruption, moral uncleanness, or vulgar speech. James exhorts Christians to “put away all filthiness,” that is, everything that is disgusting and offensive from God’s viewpoint.—2Co 7:1; 1Pe 1:14-16; 1Jo 1:9.

James now introduces another agricultural metaphor—that of planting a seed in a field. He likens Jehovah’s word to a seed planted in a person’s heart. In order for the seed to take root in him, he must “put away” what is bad. Only then can the truth of God’s Word become part of him, stabilizing his faith in God and helping him to avoid deviating from Jehovah’s righteous ways. (Col 2:6, 7 and study notes) The expression “the implanting of the word” can refer to the way in which a person first hears God’s word; however, this process is ongoing as the person continues to take in more of God’s truths. He needs to accept the word with mildness because a mild, humble, and yielding attitude makes him teachable. (Ac 17:11, 12; 1Th 2:13) When he responds to “the implanting of the word,” God’s message “is able to save” his life, as James says.
Or “your souls.”—See Glossary, “Soul.”

James urges Christians not only to hear “the word of truth” but also to apply it consistently in their life. (Jas 1:18) The tense of the Greek verb here rendered “become” highlights continuous action. As one reference work states, it means “not simply ‘be,’ but ‘show yourselves more and more.’” Another reference work explains: “James considers the practice of faith to be ongoing, something to be worked for and worked on, rather than something achieved and accomplished.” James’ words harmonize fully with what Jesus stated in his Sermon on the Mount at Mt 7:21-27.—See also Lu 11:28.

James warns Christians not to assume that merely hearing “the word of truth” is sufficient; to do so would be to deceive oneself. (Jas 1:18) According to one lexicon, the Greek word James here uses means to “delude by false reasoning.” (See also Col 2:4, where the same Greek word is rendered “delude.”) A Christian might rationalize that just professing one’s faith is enough, but that too would be false, incorrect reasoning. (Compare Jas 2:18, 20, 26.) Those who deceive themselves in that way would miss out on the blessings that come from practicing the form of worship that Jehovah approves.—Isa 48:17, 18.

This translates a Greek verb that means, not to take a quick glance, but “to consider attentively, fix one’s eyes or mind upon,” as one lexicon puts it. (Compare Heb 3:1, where the same verb is rendered “consider”; see study note.) In James’ illustration, the man has carefully examined himself and does see his problem. However, as James goes on to explain, the man fails to act on what he sees.

paragraphs.lemma: the one who peers into the perfect law
paragraphs.text: When used in its literal sense, the Greek verb here rendered “peers into” can refer to stooping forward, often in order to get a clearer view. (Joh 20:11; compare study note on 1Pe 1:12.) As used here, it means to make a thoughtful effort to find out something. “The perfect law” is a reference to “the law of the Christ.” (Ga 6:2 and study note) The person in James’ illustration does more than peer into that law; he continues in it. That Greek word suggests that he perseveres, making it a habit to ponder the perfect law and to be guided by it. Because such a Christian stays with God’s Word, God’s Word stays in him. He lives by what he learns there.

paragraphs.lemma: the perfect law that belongs to freedom
paragraphs.text: This law is superior to the Mosaic Law, which showed that imperfect humans could never on their own free themselves from enslavement to sin. (See study note on Ga 5:1.) However, “the perfect law,” that is, “the law of the Christ,” brought freedom from the written commands of the Mosaic Law. (See study notes on Ga 6:2; Col 2:14.) It made real forgiveness possible. That law belongs to freedom. It encompasses everything that Jehovah requires of us, and it offers to those who adhere to it the prospect of complete freedom from sin and from the death that results from sin.—See also study note on 2Co 3:17.
Or “is religious.” This term is related to the expression “form of worship” found in verse 27.

paragraphs.lemma: does not keep a tight rein on his tongue
paragraphs.text: Or “does not bridle his tongue.” Here James uses another vivid word picture. (Jas 1:6 and study note) He compares controlling a person’s tongue to using a bridle to control a horse. The rider controls the horse by using the bridle, that is, headgear consisting of a bit and reins. (Jas 3:2, 3; see Media Gallery, “Roman-Era ‘Bridles in the Mouths of Horses.’”) Likewise, “a worshipper of God” needs to keep his own tongue, or speech, under control. Unrestrained speech—such as slander, lying, or verbal abuse—can damage his relationship with Jehovah, even making his worship futile, or useless, unacceptable to God.—Le 19:16; Eph 4:25; Jas 3:8-10.

Or “The religion.” The Greek word (thre·skeiʹa) used here (and in verse 26, where it is rendered “worship”) could refer to a “form of worship” whether true or false. (Ac 26:5; Col 2:18 and study note) This word was often used by writers in ancient times to describe acts of worship. In this verse, James goes on to explain what form of religion is true and acceptable to God.

paragraphs.lemma: to look after orphans and widows
paragraphs.text: James here emphasizes an important feature of true worship, providing a specific example of what it means to be “a doer” of God’s word. (Jas 1:22-25) The Greek word for “look after” can also be rendered “turn one’s attention to” or “visit.” (Lu 1:68; Ac 15:14, 36) It can convey the idea of making regular visits to care for someone’s ongoing needs. (Mt 25:36, 43) In the Septuagint, this verb is often used to show how Jehovah lovingly cares for his servants. (Ru 1:6; Ps 8:4 [8:5, LXX]; Eze 34:11) So Christians were to give continuous support to those among them who were in need, such as “orphans and widows.” Jehovah had long required that his people support such ones as part of true worship.—Ex 22:22; Ps 68:5; Isa 1:10-17; Jer 7:6; compare 1Ti 5:3 and study note.

In this context, the Greek word or·pha·nosʹ refers to a child who is without at least one parent, especially the father. Back then, the father was generally the breadwinner and was responsible for the care and instruction of his children. (Eph 6:4) At times, the Greek word was used in an extended sense to refer to people in general who had suffered bereavement.—Compare study notes on Joh 14:18; 1Th 2:17.

Because of illness, a shorter lifespan, and other factors, it was common in the first century C.E. for women and children to suffer the loss of the family head. Since the man provided the primary economic support for the family, life could become truly difficult for such a household.—See study note on 2Co 1:4.

paragraphs.lemma: to keep oneself without spot from the world
paragraphs.text: James here highlights another important part of true worship. He says that Christians are to remain separate from the world, that is, unrighteous human society that is alienated from God. (See Glossary, “World.”) Jesus said that his disciples should be no part of that world. (Joh 15:19 and study note) He set the example by refusing to get involved with the world’s political and social affairs or to adopt its godless conduct and attitudes. (Mt 4:8-10; Joh 6:15; 16:33 and study note) James reminds his readers that even though they lived in the world, they were to be like Jesus—no part of it. They must not allow the world’s ways to rub off on them, thereby spotting or staining them with its godless thinking and behavior.—Jas 4:4 and study note; 1Pe 4:3, 4; 1Jo 2:15.

paragraphs.lemma: My brothers, you are not holding . . . , are you?
paragraphs.text: Or “My brothers, stop holding to the faith of our glorious Lord Jesus Christ with acts of favoritism.”

James expresses concern that some of his readers are showing special favor to the wealthy or prominent. (Jas 2:2-9) Acts of favoritism are incompatible with “holding to the faith of our glorious Lord Jesus Christ.” Followers of Christ have always been “under obligation to go on walking just as that one walked.” (1Jo 2:6) Jesus taught his disciples to treat others impartially regardless of their station in life, and he himself showed no favoritism (Lu 14:12, 13); even his opposers acknowledged this (Mt 22:15, 16). He always acted in harmony with the ways of his Father, who is impartial. (Job 34:19; Joh 12:44, 45; 14:9; Ro 2:11 and study note) God provided the ransom for rich and poor alike. (2Co 5:14, 15) And he never favors people on the basis of their wealth, race, or social status.—Le 19:15; De 1:17; Ac 10:34, 35.

paragraphs.lemma: with gold rings on his fingers
paragraphs.text: Lit., “golden-ringed.” The Greek word used here could describe a person who adorns himself with one or more gold rings. There is evidence that rich people in the first century C.E. wore many rings as a sign of their wealth and social status. For example, Roman philosopher Seneca (c. 4 B.C.E.–65 C.E.) said of his contemporaries: “We adorn our fingers with rings; a jewel is arranged on every joint.”

Here James uses the Greek word sy·na·go·geʹ, which originally referred to an assembly of people (lit., “a bringing together; an assembly”). In most of its occurrences in the Christian Greek Scriptures, this word refers to the places where the Jews met for worship and is rendered “synagogue.” (Mr 1:21; Ac 13:14; see Glossary, “Synagogue.”) In this context, however, it refers to a Christian meeting, a public gathering for worship. A related term (e·pi·sy·na·go·geʹ) is rendered “meeting together” at Heb 10:25, also with reference to Christian meetings.—See study note.

paragraphs.lemma: a poor man in filthy clothing
paragraphs.text: The men James describes in this hypothetical example are both unbelievers who attend a Christian meeting. (Compare 1Co 14:23, 24.) Despite the “filthy clothing” of this unbeliever, Christ’s example should have moved those present to welcome him impartially, no matter how shabby his appearance.—Mr 10:46-49; Lu 5:12, 13.

paragraphs.lemma: “Take that seat there under my footstool”
paragraphs.text: James here portrays a member of the congregation who is sitting in a comfortable seat with a footstool—a low stool designed to serve as a rest or support for the feet. When a wealthy visitor enters, the Christian graciously offers to give up his comfortable seat and footstool. But he contemptuously tells a poor visitor to keep standing or to sit on the floor next to the footstool, at the feet of the one sitting in the comfortable chair.—Compare Mt 23:6 and study note.

Christ himself humbly refused to judge in matters over which he had not been appointed. (Lu 12:13, 14 and study note) Yet, some Christians were acting as self-appointed judges, and they were rendering “wicked decisions”—judging the value of others based on wealth or superficial traits. As one translation says here, they were “acting like a crooked judge.” By rendering such decisions, they were promoting “class distinctions” that, in turn, would cause divisions in Jehovah’s congregation. (Ga 3:28) Judgments of that kind were truly wicked.—Mt 23:8; Joh 17:20, 21.
See study notes on Jas 1:1, 16.

paragraphs.lemma: Did not God choose those who are poor . . . ?
paragraphs.text: James does not imply that God excludes rich people from coming into a close relationship with him. (Le 19:15; compare Ac 16:14 and study note; 1Ti 6:17 and study note.) Rather, his statement reflects the reality that people who are materially poor seem to be more inclined to accept the message of the good news. (Mt 19:23, 24; 1Co 1:26-29) Poor people often suffer from the injustices of this world and thus are usually more “conscious of their spiritual need.” (Mt 5:3 and study note; Lu 6:20 and study note) In contrast, many of the rich rejected the teachings of Jesus, choosing instead to trust in material wealth.—Mr 10:20-23; Lu 6:24, 25.

paragraphs.lemma: to be rich in faith and heirs of the Kingdom
paragraphs.text: Materially poor people who accepted the good news became “rich in faith.” Real faith is a precious gift that is a product of God’s holy spirit, and it “is not a possession of all people.” (2Th 3:2 and study note; Ga 5:22) The expression “rich in faith” implies having great, or abundant, faith. Spirit-anointed Christians who exercised such faith would be “heirs of the Kingdom,” that is, they would rule together with Christ in “his heavenly Kingdom.” (2Ti 4:18) Jehovah held out this priceless opportunity to all, regardless of their financial status.

paragraphs.lemma: which he promised to those who love him
paragraphs.text: Compare study note on Jas 1:12.

Jesus Christ’s name was linked to his disciples in that they “were by divine providence called Christians.” (Ac 11:26) Jesus was sent by Jehovah, so Christians were by extension also associated with Jehovah’s name. Furthermore, the phrase by which you were called reflects a common Hebrew idiom. Commenting on this expression as used in the Hebrew Scriptures, one reference work states: “When God calls a name over someone, it means that this person becomes God’s possession and has a special relationship to him.” (De 28:10; Jer 14:9; Am 9:12; compare Ac 15:17 and study note.) Christians were in a special relationship with both Jesus and Jehovah. Yet, those first-century disciples were often persecuted by the rich class, who sought to harm their reputation, thus blaspheming “the fine name by which [they] were called.”—Ac 5:17, 18; 26:9-11; compare 1Pe 4:14, 16.

Or “the kingly law.” According to Jesus, the second greatest commandment of God’s Law to Israel was “you must love your neighbor as yourself.” (Mt 22:39 and study note; Le 19:18) The disciple James calls this command “the royal law.” This term, which is used only here in the Scriptures, is appropriate for several reasons. The law of love may be called royal because it originates from the great King, Jehovah. (1Th 4:9 and study note) In addition, it could be viewed as “royal,” or kingly, because of its prominence among other laws governing human relationships. It is a king among laws, as it were. (Ro 13:8-10; Ga 5:14) Jesus stated that this law is one of the commandments on which all the Law and the Prophets hang. (Mt 22:40 and study note) In this context, James shows that all who favored the rich over the poor were violating this “royal law.”

Christians who truly carried out “the royal law” were worthy of this commendation. It was good and right for them to show love and kindness. However, some needed to improve in showing neighborly love to the rich and the poor alike. Those favoring the rich revealed that their motives were selfish. In the context of this verse, James warns that Christians should not show partiality and favoritism in the congregation while claiming to show love. (Jas 2:1-6, 9) One reference work thus notes that such “selective love of neighbor is not love at all.” So James’ commendation here actually serves as counsel to those showing partiality. (Compare Jas 2:19.) He is saying, in effect, ‘It is fine to say that you are carrying out the royal law, but you can only do so in reality if your love is without favoritism and class distinctions.’

paragraphs.lemma: you are convicted by the law as transgressors
paragraphs.text: James is here continuing his discussion of “the royal law.” (Jas 2:8 and study note; Mt 22:39) The law about neighborly love was first recorded at Le 19:18, and in that same context, Jehovah also prohibited the showing of favoritism. (Le 19:15; see also De 1:17; 16:19.) Christ reaffirmed those laws for his followers, commanding them to love one another and to be impartial. (Mt 22:39; Joh 7:24; 13:34, 35) Here James reminds Christians that since ancient times, Jehovah has always required that his servants be impartial. So those who favored the rich over the poor, for example, were “convicted,” or reproved, for violating one of Jehovah’s long-standing requirements.—See study note on Jas 2:4; compare Ro 13:8; 1Co 13:1-3; 1Jo 4:8.

paragraphs.lemma: For if anyone obeys all the Law
paragraphs.text: James uses the Law of Moses as an example to teach Christians an important truth about “the law of the Christ.” (Ga 6:2) The phrase “all the Law” reminded readers that the Mosaic Law was not merely a collection of over 600 laws from which God’s people could pick and choose those they wanted to obey. Rather, the individual laws comprised one body of Law that governed all aspects of life. Jesus denounced the scribes and Pharisees for picking which laws to obey scrupulously while disregarding “the weightier matters of the Law.” (Mt 23:23 and study note) Clearly, Christians who showed favoritism and created class distinctions in the congregation were violating the spirit of “the royal law” that James has been discussing.—Jas 2:8.

paragraphs.lemma: you have become a transgressor of law
paragraphs.text: In this verse, James uses a vivid example to illustrate his point that the Mosaic Law was all one, a single body of sacred law. Surely none of James’ readers would argue that a man who committed murder could excuse himself by saying that he had never committed adultery. In fact, by breaking one of the Law’s commands, he made himself “an offender against all of it.” (Jas 2:10; compare Ga 3:10, 12.) Similarly, a Christian who showed partiality was a transgressor against “the royal law,” a basic feature of “the law of the Christ.”—Jas 2:8; Ga 6:2; Ac 10:34; Ro 2:11.

paragraphs.lemma: the law of a free people
paragraphs.text: Or “the law that gives freedom.” Lit., “law of freedom.” Here James refers to “the law of the Christ,” “the perfect law that belongs to freedom.” (See study notes on Ga 6:2; Jas 1:25.) It is this law, not the Mosaic Law, that God uses as the basis for judging Christians. In order to be judged favorably, they need to imitate Jesus’ example in the way they speak and act, obeying his teachings. That gives them the prospect of complete freedom from sin and death, something the Mosaic Law could never provide.—Ps 130:3, 4; Joh 8:32, 36; Ro 8:2-4; Ga 5:22, 23.

The context shows that James here speaks of the mercy that Christians are to show toward others. (Jas 1:27; 2:1-9, 14-17) Jehovah commanded his people to show mercy not only by forgiving others but also by helping those in need. (Pr 21:13; Zec 7:9; Mt 5:7 and study note; 12:7; 18:21, 22; compare Lu 10:36, 37.) When rendering an account to God, sinful humans who have been merciful can be confident that he, in turn, will show mercy to them. (Mt 6:12 and study note, 14, 15; 7:2) Thus the merciful conduct of Christians triumphs, or wins out, over any adverse judgment that might have been brought on them.—See study note on Jas 3:17.

paragraphs.lemma: That faith cannot save him, can it?
paragraphs.text: James knows, of course, that Christians are “saved through faith”—that they cannot please God without it. (Eph 2:8; Heb 11:6 and study note) Here, though, James stresses that genuine faith is always accompanied by works, examples of which are found in the next two verses. Without such works, James says, a Christian’s faith would be “dead,” or “useless.” (Jas 2:15-17, 20) Some have claimed that James’ words contradict what Paul said about Christians being “declared righteous by faith” rather than “works of law.” (Ro 3:28; Ga 2:16) Actually, James’ teaching on faith harmonizes with that of Paul, who likewise taught that genuine faith shows itself in actions. (Eph 2:10; Heb 11:1, 4, 7-9, 17, 24-28, 31) Paul stressed that Christians must exercise faith in Jesus Christ and obey “the law of the Christ”; this is essential for salvation. (Ga 6:2; 2Ti 3:15) However, Paul also warned against those who insisted that Christians must still have the kind of “works” that were now worthless—those performed in obedience to the outdated Mosaic Law code. (Ro 3:20) So James’ forceful explanation here—that genuine faith must be accompanied by Christian works—is a vital complement to the teachings of Paul.

James uses the expression “brothers or sisters” to refer to fellow Christians. Although the expression “brothers” was often used to refer to all in the congregation, here he specifically mentions “sisters” as well. (Compare study notes on Ac 1:15; Ro 1:13; 1Co 9:5.) In contrast with the way women were often viewed in James’ day, the Christian congregation appreciated both men and women and cared for their needs.—Ga 6:10; Jas 1:27; compare study notes on 1Ti 5:3, 9.
Lit., “naked.” The Greek word here used (gy·mnosʹ) can have the meaning “lacking adequate clothing,” “poorly dressed.”—See study notes on Mt 25:36; 1Co 4:11.

The Greek word here rendered “enough . . . for the day” could refer to “the day’s supply” of food for a particular day. However, it is likely that the word here implies not merely a temporary condition but a constant lack of sufficient daily food. James seems to describe brothers or sisters whose basic needs, such as clothing and food, are not met.

This phrase was a customary Jewish expression of farewell, a wish for well-being. (Mr 5:34 and study note; Lu 7:50) However, to use the phrase when talking to someone in need—and even adding “keep warm and well fed”—without offering any practical help would be useless, perhaps even hypocritical.

paragraphs.lemma: faith by itself, without works, is dead
paragraphs.text: See study notes on Jas 2:14, 26.

James here introduces an imaginary “someone” to further his point on the relationship between faith and works. He apparently has in mind “someone” responding to an objector who insists that works are not necessary in order to demonstrate true faith. To answer that objection, the imaginary “someone” presents this challenge: ‘You may claim to show me your supposed faith without works, but I will show you my faith by my works.’ The point is: Any person who claims to have faith but who has no works to show his faith in action would not actually have real faith. His supposed faith would be a mere sham. However, because the original Greek text does not use quotation marks, some translations present this dialogue as if “someone” is objecting to James’ argument and James himself replies. Regardless of how the dialogue is understood, the point is the same: Real faith is shown by works.

With this statement, James argues forcefully that mere belief in God’s existence is not enough to save a person. The rebel spirits known as demons are absolutely certain that “there is one God.” They served in God’s glorious presence before rebelling against him. (Jude 6 and study note) So there are no atheists or agnostics among them. Yet, they have no true faith. Their belief in the simple fact of God’s existence gives them no comfort and certainly no hope.—Compare Lu 8:31 and study note.

Lit., “they are bristling up.” The Greek word can be used regarding humans as well as animals when their hair stands on end, such as from fear. (Compare Job 4:15 and Jer 2:12 where the same Greek word is used figuratively in the Septuagint.) Here James does not refer to the kind of wholesome, godly fear, or respectful awe, that moves a faithful servant of God to reject what is bad. (Compare study note on Heb 5:7.) Rather, James refers to the sickening dread that the demons have of the all-powerful One who has promised to subject them to the punishment that they rightly deserve.—Compare Mt 8:28, 29; Lu 4:33, 34; 2Pe 2:4; Jude 6 and study note.

James directs his words to an imaginary opponent who believes that faith alone is enough. The apostle Paul uses a similar rhetorical technique in his letters. (Ro 2:1; 9:20; 1Co 15:36) One reference work states that this was a common method of argument in ancient times. James calls this hypothetical man “empty”; he lacks accurate knowledge of God and a true understanding of his Word. By addressing an imaginary opponent, James does not offend his readers but helps them to avoid adopting wrong views.

In the preceding verse, James has made the point that even the demons have a form of belief in God; they acknowledge that he exists and shudder at his power to destroy them. (See study notes on Jas 2:19.) But James’ readers knew well that the demons are far from having the kind of faith that pleases God. Whatever belief in Jehovah the demons have is worthless; it will never move them to do anything good or righteous.—See study note on Jas 2:14.

This term translates a Greek word that could literally be rendered “idle.” Without works, faith is inactive and unprofitable; it is as unproductive and wasteful as a laborer who refuses to do the work he was hired for.—Compare Tit 1:12, where the same Greek word is rendered “idle.”

paragraphs.lemma: Was not Abraham our father declared righteous by works . . . ?
paragraphs.text: According to the Genesis account, when Abraham put faith in God’s promise to make his offspring numerous, like the stars of heaven, Jehovah “counted it to him as righteousness.” (Ge 15:5, 6; Ro 4:3 and study note; Jas 2:23 and study note) Decades later, Abraham further demonstrated his faith “by works” in a most extraordinary way; he showed that he was ready to offer up his son Isaac. (Ge 22:10-12) For this reason, James could say that Abraham was “declared righteous by works after he offered up Isaac his son on the altar” and that Abraham’s “faith was perfected by his works.”—Jas 2:22 and study notes.

Although James was of Jewish descent, he was writing to Christians of all backgrounds, both Jewish and Gentile. (See study note on Jas 1:1.) So he could not here have been referring to Abraham as the natural ancestor of the Jews. Rather, he mentions Abraham in the same sense that Paul did when calling him “the father of all those having faith.” (Ro 4:11 and study note, 12) Jesus himself told natural Jews that only those “doing the works of Abraham” could rightfully claim to be Abraham’s children. (Joh 8:39) Therefore, all faithful Christians, regardless of their background, can view Abraham as their father.—Ga 3:7 and study note, 28 and study note, 29.

In the Christian Greek Scriptures, being “declared righteous” usually refers to spirit-anointed Christians; they are acquitted of sin and adopted as sons by Jehovah, based on the ransom sacrifice of Jesus. (Ro 3:24 and study note; 5:17, 18; 8:30; Tit 3:7) As a result, they can rule with Christ in heaven. (Re 20:6) Abraham, however, lived long before that heavenly hope was offered to any human, so he must have been “declared righteous” in a different sense. In verse 23, James says that Abraham “came to be called Jehovah’s friend.” Therefore, Abraham was “declared righteous,” not as a spirit-anointed son of God, but as a friend of God.—2Ch 20:7; Isa 41:8.

By using the expression “offered up . . . on the altar,” James apparently means that Abraham went as far as binding his son Isaac and putting him on the altar; Abraham was ready to sacrifice him. (Ge 22:9-12; compare study note on Heb 11:17.) By his willingness to offer up Isaac, Abraham demonstrated his faith, obedience, and deep love for God.

paragraphs.lemma: his faith was active along with his works
paragraphs.text: James is apparently using a play on the Greek words for “was active along with” and “works,” and the whole phrase could be translated “his faith was working together with his works.” James’ point is that faith and works should combine to complement and support each other. Abraham believed in God’s promise, recorded at Ge 12:1-3, from the time he first received it. He then showed his faith by obeying God’s command to go out from his land; he “went just as Jehovah had told him.” (Ge 12:4) Abraham based the whole course of his life on his faith that God’s promises were sure to be fulfilled.

paragraphs.lemma: and his faith was perfected by his works
paragraphs.text: The Greek word rendered “was perfected” can mean “to make something complete” or “to cause it to reach its goal.” One lexicon says that in this context, the word conveys the idea that Abraham’s faith was “made such as it ought to be.” For faith to be real, genuine, or complete, it must be accompanied by good deeds and obedience to God. Abraham had faith that “God was able to raise [Isaac] up even from the dead” and fulfill His promises involving Isaac and his promised offspring. (Heb 11:19 and study note) Without such faith, Abraham would surely not have attempted to offer up his son. (Heb 11:17) It was by Abraham’s works, carried out in complete obedience to God, that “his faith was perfected,” or made complete.—Compare Heb 12:2 and study note.

In this quote from Ge 15:6, the divine name, represented by four Hebrew consonants (transliterated YHWH), occurs in the original Hebrew text. Existing Greek manuscripts of James’ letter have the word The·osʹ (God) here, perhaps reflecting the term used at Ge 15:6 in available manuscripts of the Septuagint. This use of “God” in Greek manuscripts may explain why most translations say “God” here. However, the original Hebrew text from which this quotation is taken contains the Tetragrammaton, and therefore the divine name is used in the main text of the New World Translation. The whole phrase taken from Ge 15:6 is also quoted at Ro 4:3 and Ga 3:6.—See App. C1 and C2.

paragraphs.lemma: it was counted to him as righteousness
paragraphs.text: Abraham’s faith was “counted [or, “credited; attributed”] to him as righteousness” by Jehovah, according to the words of Ge 15:6. Thus God viewed Abraham as guiltless in a relative sense. (Ro 4:3 and study note) But that declaration of Jehovah was fulfilled, or verified, when Abraham further proved his faith by works. His willingness to offer up Isaac, the offspring that God had promised him, demonstrated that Abraham’s faith in God was unwavering.—Ge 22:12.

paragraphs.lemma: and he came to be called Jehovah’s friend
paragraphs.text: James here refers to the most precious friendship that any human can enjoy. Abraham put faith in Jehovah and proved it by obedience. Jehovah, in turn, showed in various ways that Abraham was His friend. For example, Jehovah did so when he openly revealed his intentions regarding Sodom. (Ge 18:17; compare Joh 15:15 and study note.) Jehovah honored his friendship with Abraham throughout the man’s life and has loyally continued to do so.—Ge 18:19, 23-33; 22:12; Ex 3:6; Isa 41:8; Mt 22:31, 32.

James may here be alluding to the two instances in the Hebrew Scriptures in which Abraham is called God’s friend. (2Ch 20:7; Isa 41:8) The Hebrew expression used in those two verses literally means “one who loves.” In the case of Abraham, the term refers to a loving and beloved friend. The friendship between God and his beloved servant was marked on both sides by loyalty, trust, and open communication. Here at Jas 2:23, James uses the Greek word phiʹlos (friend), which is related to the verb meaning “to have affection for.”—See study notes on Joh 5:20; 16:27; for the use of the divine name here, see App. C3 introduction; Jas 2:23.

paragraphs.lemma: declared righteous by works and not by faith alone
paragraphs.text: See study note on Jas 2:14; see also study note on Ga 2:16.

Remarkably, James says that Jehovah declared “Rahab the prostitute” righteous “in the same manner” as He did “the father of all those having faith,” Abraham. (Ro 4:11 and study note; Jas 2:21 and study note) That Rahab is mentioned favorably right along with Abraham exemplifies James’ own inspired counsel, recorded earlier in this letter, in which he condemns class distinctions and partiality in the congregation. (Jas 2:1 and study note, 4) Jesus too reflected his Father’s impartiality in the way he treated sincere individuals who were looked down on by society in general.—Mt 21:31, 32.

Rahab was a prostitute living in an idolatrous nation, but Jehovah took note of her outstanding faith in him as the true God. (Jos 2:1, 9-11) Risking her life, Rahab courageously hid the Israelite spies and thus backed up her faith by works. (Jos 2:4, 16, 21-23; see study note on Heb 11:31.) Therefore, as James points out here, Rahab was declared righteous by works. That is, Jehovah viewed Rahab as guiltless, although she was an imperfect human. (Compare study notes on Jas 2:21.) Rahab is one of the five women mentioned in the genealogy of Jesus.—Mt 1:5; compare study note on Mt 1:3.

The Greek word here rendered “spirit” may also be translated “breath.” (See Glossary, “Spirit.”) It refers here to the force that animates the body, making it live. (Compare Lu 8:55 and study note.) James’ point: Just as a body without spirit, or breath of life, is dead, so faith without works is dead, or useless and ineffective. This reasoning would have been powerful to Christians familiar with the Hebrew Scriptures. As one reference work states, the Hebrews “knew nothing of the immortality of the soul and the possibility of its being independent of the body.” In fact, the Hebrew Scriptures repeatedly make the point that the dead are incapable of doing anything. (Ps 115:17; 146:3, 4; Ec 9:5, 10) None of James’ readers would have wanted faith that was dead.

paragraphs.lemma: Not many of you should become teachers
paragraphs.text: Here James addresses men who were reaching out for a divinely appointed role—that of being a teacher in the congregation. (1Co 12:28, 29; Eph 4:11) However, some may ambitiously have sought this role, viewing it as a position of prominence. (Compare 1Ti 1:7 and study note.) It seems that some even set themselves up as teachers, although not being appointed or qualified to be such. Thus, James warns against becoming a teacher for the wrong reasons. He goes on to emphasize the seriousness of the assignment; it should not be taken lightly. (Lu 12:48) But James was not discouraging brothers from “reaching out to be an overseer, . . . qualified to teach” in the congregation—as long as they did so with the proper motive.—1Ti 3:1 and study note, 2.
See study note on Jas 1:16.

Or “stricter judgment.” All Christians will render an account to God, but here James points out that teachers in the congregation, himself included, will be judged more strictly. (Ro 14:12) God holds teachers to a higher standard because their speech and conduct can greatly influence others in the congregation—for better or for worse.—Lu 12:48; Heb 13:17.

The verb “to stumble” is used figuratively here, and this clause could be translated “we all make many mistakes.” By using the pronoun “we,” James humbly includes himself to show that no imperfect human is exempt from error. (1Ki 8:46; Jas 3:1; 1Jo 1:8) In the preceding verse, James explained that teachers “will receive heavier judgment.” Here he gives one reason: Like all imperfect humans, teachers often stumble in word, that is, they err in what they say. Because their words affect others, for good or for bad, teachers in particular must bridle their tongue, that is, control their speech.
See study note on Jas 1:26.

This expression translates a Greek word that in its literal sense refers to someone who keeps something on a straight course. In this context, it refers to a helmsman who steers a ship on its course. The related Greek verb is rendered “make . . . straight” at Joh 1:23.

paragraphs.lemma: The tongue is also a fire
paragraphs.text: This vivid metaphor drives home the point of the preceding sentence. (Jas 3:5; compare Isa 9:18.) The tongue, though a small body member, can be like a fire that spreads quickly and does tremendous damage. James’ strong words in these verses suggest that he may have seen the harm caused by misuse of the gift of speech, whether a bragging claim, a harsh judgment driven by jealousy, or some other divisive remark. (Jas 3:14, 16) When misused in such ways, the tongue can hurt feelings, tarnish reputations, and shatter trust—sometimes beyond repair.—See also Pr 16:27; 26:20, 21.

paragraphs.lemma: The tongue represents a world of unrighteousness
paragraphs.text: When uncontrolled, the human tongue represents, or constitutes, a world of every sort of evil and unrighteousness. Misuse of the tongue includes slander, obscenity, false testimony, misrepresentation, reviling, deceptive propaganda, and all forms of erroneous teaching. One reference work thus states: “The tongue, we may say, is the embodiment of all wrong. It utters every wrong emotion and thought and puts every kind of a wrong deed into words.” Some scholars suggest that in this context, the phrase “a world of” can mean “a tremendous amount of.” Certainly, the misuse of the tongue contributes greatly to the evil of this world that is alienated from God.

Uncontrolled bad speech defiles not only a man’s tongue but also his whole being. Such misuse of the tongue reveals what a person is inside—the condition of his figurative heart. Jesus made a similar point when he said: “Whatever comes out of the mouth comes from the heart, and those things defile a man.”—Mt 15:18, 19.

paragraphs.lemma: and sets the whole course of life on fire
paragraphs.text: “The whole course of life” renders a Greek phrase that literally means “the wheel of the birth (origin).” The idea seems to be that if a person fails to control his tongue, this little organ can cause damage over the entire course of his life, from youth to old age. One reference work suggests that the literal wording used here may have brought to mind the image of a chariot wheel spinning so fast that the axle at its center heats up and ignites. Such a fire would quickly spread to engulf the whole wheel.—Compare Mr 7:20-23; Ro 3:9-14.

paragraphs.lemma: it is set on fire by Gehenna
paragraphs.text: Decades earlier, Jesus used the fire of Gehenna as a symbol of everlasting destruction. (Mt 5:22 and study note; see also Glossary, “Gehenna.”) Here James stresses a sobering truth: The Christian who misuses his tongue could lose God’s favor and even face the sad end of being erased from existence forever. (Compare Mt 12:31, 32, 37.) In a sense, a person’s misuse of his tongue by his vile speech could bring on him the destructive power of Gehenna. So his hateful words could do more than cause damage to others; they could make him a victim of the fire that he himself started.—Compare Mt 23:33.

The Greek verb rendered “is to be tamed” seems to convey the idea “can be tamed,” expressing a timeless fact or truth. And as James states next (“has been tamed”), humans have indeed trained and subdued a wide variety of wild creatures. This is in harmony with Jehovah’s original decree that mankind should “have in subjection” the various kinds of wild animals, birds, reptiles, and sea creatures mentioned in the Genesis account of creation.—Ge 1:24-28.

In the Hebrew Scriptures, Jehovah God was at times referred to as the Father of his earthly servants. (Isa 63:16; 64:8; Mal 2:10) However, when Jesus was on earth, he primarily addressed Jehovah as Father and he taught his followers to do the same. (Mt 5:16 and study note; 6:9 and study note) Additionally, Jehovah is the Father of all humans in the sense that they all owe their existence to him as their Creator and the original Life-Giver.—Ac 17:22, 25-29; for the use of the divine name in this verse, see App. C3 introduction; Jas 3:9.
See Glossary; see also study note on “in the likeness of God” in this verse.

James here refers to the Genesis account, which states that God made the first human couple “in his image.” (Ge 1:26, 27) They were therefore like God, not in physical appearance (Lu 24:39; Joh 4:24), but in that they possessed similar qualities, such as love, wisdom, and a sense of justice. Likewise, the psalmist David was inspired to show that God created humans with a measure of dignity, glory, and honor. (Ps 8:1, 4, 5) The Bible indicates that even imperfect descendants of Adam can reflect God’s qualities to some degree, especially when they put on “the new personality.” (Col 3:10 and study note; Ac 28:1, 2; Ro 2:13-15) So the point James here makes is that those who curse, or speak disrespectfully of, fellow humans insult God, since humans are made “in the likeness of God.” On the other hand, those who praise, or speak well of, fellow humans in effect acknowledge God as the Source of human dignity.

paragraphs.lemma: A spring does not cause the fresh water and the bitter water to bubble out of the same opening
paragraphs.text: In this verse and in the following one, James uses three powerful illustrations to support the point that he has just made: “It is not right” for a Christian to use his mouth to utter both healthful speech and harmful speech. (Jas 3:10) First, he contrasts water that is “fresh,” or clear and drinkable (lit., “sweet”), with water that is “bitter,” or distasteful and unsafe to drink. (Compare Ex 15:23; Re 8:11.) A spring would not alternate between producing drinkable and undrinkable water. It would yield either one or the other. Thus James suggests that it would be unnatural and, by implication, even hypocritical for a Christian to use his mouth to utter both healthful speech and harmful speech.

paragraphs.lemma: a fig tree cannot produce olives, or a grapevine figs, can it?
paragraphs.text: James continues to use well-known commodities from everyday life to illustrate important lessons. One reference work notes: “Figs, olives and grapes were the three most common agricultural products of the Judean hills, and alongside wheat and barley they would have constituted the most common crops of the Mediterranean region as a whole.” James’ statement here is in agreement with God’s unchangeable law that “trees [yield] fruit . . . according to their kinds.” (Ge 1:11, 12) The point James makes is that the tree or the vine would produce only the fruit that God intended it to produce. So with this illustration, James again emphasizes that misuse of the tongue is contrary to what is natural and fitting.—Compare Mt 7:16-19 and Media Gallery, “Fig Tree, Grapevine, and Thornbush.”

paragraphs.lemma: Neither can salt water produce fresh water
paragraphs.text: Salt water, such as seawater, is not fit for drinking, and it will not change into clear, drinkable water. One reference work expresses it: “While fresh water added to salt water does not produce fresh water, salt water added to fresh causes the water to be salty. The poison of the tongue is all-pervasive.” When the person who should bring forth wholesome words also persistently produces hurtful words, something is wrong. The person who uses his tongue in that way can do great harm to others. Each of James’ examples on this subject suggests that humans who use cruel speech are acting in a way that is not only unkind but even unnatural—out of harmony with the intent of their Creator.

paragraphs.lemma: Who is wise and understanding among you?
paragraphs.text: With this rhetorical question, James introduces his discussion on what characterizes true wisdom as opposed to earthly wisdom. (Jas 3:13-18; see study notes on Jas 3:15, 17.) Christians who have “the wisdom from above” know how to apply knowledge and understanding from God in a way that brings good results. (Pr 2:10-15; 9:10; Jas 1:5) James may especially have had in mind elders who serve as teachers in the congregation. (Jas 3:1, 2) However, the question James here poses could rightly be directed to all worshippers of Jehovah; all need to examine themselves to see whether they display the wisdom from God. (Jas 3:17) Later in this chapter, James explains that Christians show godly wisdom not only in their speech but also in their everyday conduct.

As used in this context, the terms “wise” and “understanding” complement each other. (Compare Job 28:12; Jer 10:12; Ho 14:9.) According to one lexicon, the Greek word here rendered “understanding” describes a person who is “knowledgeable, well-instructed, skilled.” A wise person would know how to apply such understanding. The Greek words for “wise and understanding” occur together in the Septuagint, for example, at De 1:13, 15; 4:6.

paragraphs.lemma: with a mildness that comes from wisdom
paragraphs.text: James shows here that mildness comes as a result of genuine, godly wisdom, “the wisdom from above.” (Jas 3:17) He suggests that when Christians ask God for such wisdom and apply it, they will display genuine mildness in what they say and do, thus promoting peace. (Eph 4:1-3; Jas 1:5) Those who wish to qualify as teachers in the congregation need both mildness and wisdom in order to be effective and useful in this vital work. (Jas 3:1, 2) Such teachers are to be, not arrogant or opinionated, but gentle, calm, and peaceful. (2Ti 2:24 and study note, 25 and study note) Christian mildness is the opposite of the qualities James refers to next.—Jas 3:14-16.

The Greek term used here for “jealousy” refers to negative feelings over someone else’s accomplishments or success. (Pr 14:30; see study note on Ga 5:20.) James describes such jealousy as being “bitter”—the same word he used in verse 11 to describe undrinkable water. Such bitter jealousy could be fueled by a person’s inordinate desire to outshine others in teaching ability and displays of wisdom.

The Greek word that James here uses can refer to a mental attitude or tendency that leads to quarreling and strife. The apostle Paul used the same Greek word to describe one of “the works of the flesh” mentioned at Ga 5:19, 20, where it is rendered “dissensions.” Some scholars suggest that this word could also be rendered “selfish ambition.” Prideful, selfish ambition often breeds contentions. An ambitious person tends to quarrel with others, creating strife as he tries to gain greater influence or prominence. James thus urges his readers to avoid such a spirit. Instead, they should promote peace and unity in the congregation. James uses the phrase in your hearts to stress that the root of such problems lies in the treacherous heart of sinful humans.—Jer 17:9; Mt 15:18.

paragraphs.lemma: do not be bragging and lying against the truth
paragraphs.text: James here reproves certain men, especially teachers in the congregation, who claimed to be “wise and understanding” but were actually contentious, motivated by bitter jealousy and selfish ambition. (Jas 3:13) They were “lying against the truth,” that is, Christian truth as revealed in the inspired Scriptures. They claimed to represent Jehovah but failed to display the wisdom that comes from him. (Jas 3:17 and study notes) In fact, such men misrepresented the truth, which clearly condemned their behavior. (Ga 5:26; Php 2:3) They also failed to meet the qualifications for Christian teachers as set forth in God’s Word.—1Ti 3:3 and study note; Tit 3:2 and study note; compare Jer 9:23, 24.

In this verse, James describes a kind of wisdom that produces pride and jealousy and that is in opposition to “the wisdom from above.” (Jas 3:14, 17 and study note) He uses three progressively stronger expressions, the most emphatic being “demonic.” James first calls this wisdom “earthly.” In the Bible, this term is used to contrast physical things with heavenly things. (Joh 3:12; 1Co 15:40) In this context, it describes the thinking of sinful humans alienated from God. It also suggests the idea of being in opposition to God’s spirit.—Php 3:19; Col 3:2 and study note.

The second term that James uses to describe ungodly wisdom (psy·khi·kosʹ) is rendered “physical” in some contexts. For example, the apostle Paul used this Greek term to refer to a person who has no interest in or appreciation for spiritual matters. (1Co 2:14 and study note, 15 and study note) In rendering this term, some translations use the adjective “animal.” One reference work offers this definition of the Greek word: “Occupied with mere animal things, animal, sensual.” Such so-called wisdom is “animalistic,” being the product of fleshly inclinations. James here uses this term to describe how such fleshly inclinations can cause a person to think and behave in an ungodly way, even like an unreasoning animal.—Ps 73:22; compare study note on Jude 19.

This is the strongest word that James uses to describe false wisdom, showing that such wisdom reflects the disposition of the demons, spirit enemies of God.—1Ti 4:1; Re 16:14; see also study note on Eph 6:12.
Or possibly, “selfish ambition.”—See study note on Jas 3:14.

The Greek word here rendered “disorder” can refer to instability, confusion, and tumult. (See study note on Lu 21:9.) Earlier in this chapter, James used a related Greek word to describe the untamable tongue as “unruly.” (Jas 3:8) The apostle Paul stated that Jehovah “is a God not of disorder but of peace.” (1Co 14:33 and study note) By contrasting “peace” with “disorder,” Paul emphasized that disorder has no place in the congregation.

The term here rendered “vile” can refer to something bad, evil, contemptible. (See study note on 2Co 5:10, where the same Greek word occurs.) James identifies “disorder and every vile thing” as harmful consequences of jealousy and contentiousness. Both qualities characterize thinking that is “earthly, animalistic, demonic.” (Jas 3:15) As James warns in the following chapter, such traits can bring conflict and wickedness into the congregation.—Jas 4:1-3; compare 2Co 12:20; Ga 5:15.

James here opens his description of “the wisdom from above [or “from heaven”],” that is, wisdom that comes from God himself. (1Co 1:21, 30; Eph 3:10; compare Joh 19:11, where the Greek word rendered “from above” also appears; see study note.) James goes on to list eight characteristics of divine wisdom, showing how it affects the actions, thinking, and motives of a person who allows himself to be guided by it. However, this list is not exhaustive; it does not cover every quality that divine wisdom can produce. (Compare study note on Ga 5:23.) A person who lives according to the wisdom from above resists developing any traits that are “earthly, animalistic, demonic,” such as those mentioned in the preceding verses. (Jas 3:14-16) The wisdom that comes from God is distinctly different from worldly wisdom, which is foolishness from Jehovah’s standpoint.—1Co 1:18-21.

It is fitting that James says that godly wisdom is “first of all pure” because everything about Jehovah God, its Source, is “pure” and “holy.” (1Jo 3:3; 1Pe 1:16) The wise guidance from his Word is described as “pure” and “refined.” (Ps 12:6) Because godly wisdom is pure, the thoughts, desires, and motives of a person who has this wisdom are clean and upright. (Pr 2:10-12; 4:23; compare 1Ti 1:5 and study note.) His heart is not corrupted by the “earthly, animalistic, demonic” thinking of this world. (Jas 3:15) Such a pure, clean heart can reflect the other qualities that James uses to describe the wisdom from above.—Jas 3:14 and study note; see also study notes on Mt 5:8; Php 4:8.

After saying that the wisdom from above is “first of all pure,” James lists qualities that reflect such purity and holiness. One reference work states: “The seven qualities that follow in the list are specific dimensions of this overall purity.” James’ point is that godly wisdom affects a person’s thinking and outlook in all areas of life.
