Christians who are guided by divine wisdom “pursue peace with all people.” (Heb 12:14 and study note; Mt 5:9 and study note; Ga 5:22) They reject the kind of thinking that would move them to promote themselves; they do not want to disrupt peace by making others feel inferior or jealous. They are quick to forgive, and they do not selfishly insist on their rights and preferences. However, James did not mean that Christians would always have peaceful relations with everyone. In fact, Paul offered this balanced counsel: “If possible, as far as it depends on you, be peaceable with all men.”—Ro 12:18.

Lit., “yielding.” The Greek word James here uses can be rendered in a variety of ways and may refer to being gentle, considerate, kind, or tolerant. As the Source of “the wisdom from above,” Jehovah God is reasonable. James was likely familiar with the use of this Greek term to describe Jehovah. The psalmist David was inspired to call Jehovah “ready to forgive,” and in the Septuagint translation, that expression is rendered with the same word that James here uses for “reasonable.” (Ps 86:5 [85:5, LXX]) He thus makes a forceful point: If the Sovereign of the universe is reasonable, ready to forgive, surely no human has any basis to think that he is above cultivating this appealing quality.—See also study notes on Php 4:5; 1Ti 3:3.

A person who has wisdom from God does not obey just out of obligation but is ready and eager to adhere to Jehovah’s standards and to follow the guidance He provides in the Scriptures. (Ro 6:17) A person who shows such willing obedience to God would also be willing to cooperate with others. One reference work notes: “Unlike competitive worldly wisdom, the wisdom from above is ‘obedient’ and lends itself to cooperation.”—Compare study note on Heb 13:17.

A merciful person does more than feel compassion for others; he also takes action to meet their needs. For example, Jesus taught that the one who acts mercifully is impelled by compassion to give practical help to a man who had been brutally beaten. (Lu 10:29-37; Jas 2:13 and study note) A person who is “full of mercy” is filled with sympathetic thoughts and feelings. Those, in turn, move him to act in a merciful, kind way. Such conduct reflects “the wisdom from above,” for Jehovah is “rich in mercy.”—Eph 2:4.

“Good fruits” refer to actions that are in harmony with “goodness and righteousness and truth.” (Eph 5:9) James here mentions “mercy” and “good fruits” together. Mercy often involves an active concern for others, so this form of compassion naturally produces a rich crop of kindly deeds. (See study note on Mt 5:7.) A person who is governed by divine wisdom will generously do good things for others.—Heb 13:16.

The Greek word here rendered “impartial” can convey the idea of being “free from prejudice” and “not being judgmental or divisive.” Earlier in his letter, James pointed out that showing favoritism is a sin. (Jas 2:1-9) Here he indicates that a person who is guided by “the wisdom from above” strives to be impartial in his dealings with others, especially those in the Christian congregation. He does not make distinctions or treat some people better than others on the basis of superficial characteristics, such as wealth or prominence.
The Greek word here used also appears at 1Ti 1:5, where it is rendered “without hypocrisy.”—See study note; see also study notes on Lu 6:42; 1Pe 1:22.

James here uses an expression that is also found elsewhere in the Scriptures. (Am 6:12; Heb 12:11 and study note) He contrasts this beautiful fruitage of godly wisdom with the rotten fruitage of false wisdom—including jealousy, contentiousness, and disorder. (Jas 3:13-17) He indicates that this “fruit of righteousness is sown” by Christians working hard to maintain peace in the congregation. James’ word picture is brief, for he speaks of sowing fruitage instead of seed. The idea may be that Christians both sow and reap righteousness. They sow righteousness by obeying God and living up to his righteous standards; they reap righteous “fruit,” such as peace, because Jehovah blesses their efforts. James goes on to show that such good fruitage results when there are “peaceful conditions” in the congregation.—See study note on Ga 6:7.

Or possibly, “by.” The rendering “for” indicates that the reward for those making peace is “the fruit of righteousness.” (See study note those who are making peace in this verse.) Some Bible translations render this phrase “by those who are making peace,” indicating that those making peace are the ones who sow this fruit of righteousness. It is possible that James had both meanings in mind.

James has just shown that righteousness flourishes where there are “peaceful conditions.” Here he alludes to the responsibility that each member of the congregation has in helping to create such a climate by “making peace.” The idea seems to be that those who act as peacemakers will also enjoy the fruit of their own work. (Compare Isa 32:17; Zec 8:12.) James’ statement calls to mind Jesus’ words in his famous Sermon on the Mount: “Happy are the peacemakers, since they will be called sons of God.”—Mt 5:9 and study note; compare Ro 12:18.

The Greek word here rendered “wars” can refer to an ongoing state of conflict, or a military campaign, while the word for “fights” refers to individual battles in a war. As elsewhere in the Bible, such military language is used metaphorically. (1Ti 1:18; 2Ti 2:23, 24 and study note; compare 2Co 10:4.) So James uses strong figurative language to show that strife and conflict were, in effect, turning Christ’s congregation into a battlefield. Some apparently engaged in verbal battles or showed a warlike spirit as they vied for greater influence in the congregation. Their combative attitude was in stark contrast to the peaceable, reasonable spirit produced by “the wisdom from above” that James has just discussed.—Jas 3:17 and study notes, 18 and study note.

paragraphs.lemma: your fleshly desires that carry on a conflict
paragraphs.text: The Greek word here rendered “fleshly desires” can refer to a strong selfish craving for pleasure of some kind. (See Lu 8:14, where this Greek word is rendered “pleasures.”) James may have had in mind a craving not only for immoral pleasures but also for such things as wealth, prestige, or the power to influence or control others. He again uses military language, this time by saying that fleshly desires can “carry on a conflict,” a phrase that literally refers to a military campaign. Selfish desires can become like an attacking army, inflicting terrible damage. James explains that such desires, if not restrained, could cause “wars and fights” among Christians. Such desires could even rob them of their relationship with God.

Lit., “in your members.” Fleshly desires originate from within. (Compare Jas 1:14, 15.) The apostle Paul expressed it similarly when he said: “I see in my body [lit., “in my members”] another law warring against the law of my mind and leading me captive to sin’s law that is in my body.”—Ro 7:23; see also study note on Ro 6:13.

paragraphs.lemma: You desire, and yet you do not have
paragraphs.text: Evidently, some first-century Christians failed to control their selfish desires. Since God would not fulfill those desires, they kept fighting one another in an effort to obtain what they craved. (La 3:44; Jas 4:1, 3) If their desires had been in harmony with his will, Jehovah would have been delighted to be generous with those Christians.—Jas 1:17; 1Jo 5:14.

It seems that some Christians were nurturing such intense jealousy and hatred that James says that they were “murdering.” Clearly, James was speaking figuratively; any unrepentant murderers would have been removed from the congregation. (1Co 5:13) If a person failed to correct his hostile, hateful attitude, Jehovah might eventually judge him as a murderer.—Compare Mt 5:22 and study note.
Or “and are jealous.”—See study note on 1Co 13:4, where the same Greek word is rendered “jealous.”

paragraphs.lemma: you do not receive because you are asking for a wrong purpose
paragraphs.text: Some of James’ readers were primarily concerned with satisfying their own desires. So they prayed with no concern about God’s will or about how others might be affected. If Jehovah did give them something, they would probably not appreciate it and would use it in selfish ways. Therefore, Jehovah did not grant their requests. (Compare Isa 1:15.) Jehovah answers only those who seek to live in harmony with his will and who want to help others.—Pr 28:9; Mt 7:11; 1Jo 3:22.

Or “You unfaithful ones.” In the Hebrew Scriptures, Jehovah spoke of the nation of Israel as his wife because that nation was in a covenant relationship with him. However, when Israel turned to other gods or made alliances with other nations, God’s people became an unfaithful wife, an adulteress. (Jer 3:1, 8, 20; Eze 16:15, 25-29; Ho 4:15; 9:1) Jesus used a similar expression regarding unfaithful ones in his day. (Mt 12:39; Mr 8:38 and study note) James indicates that dedicated Christians who became friends of the world were unfaithful to God, committing spiritual adultery.—Joh 17:14; 2Co 11:2; Re 14:4.

In the preceding verses, James referred to wrong attitudes that some Christians had. (Jas 4:1-3) In fact, their actions resembled the ways of the wicked world around them. James here uses a pointed rhetorical question to help those Christians realize that their attitudes were making them friends of the world.

paragraphs.lemma: friendship with the world is enmity with God
paragraphs.text: In this context, “the world” refers to the wicked human society that is alienated from God. (Jas 1:27; 1Jo 2:15-17; see Glossary, “World.”) “Friendship [Greek, phi·liʹa] with the world” indicates an emotional attachment to it. Friends of the world would develop the dominant attitude that permeates the world. (Eph 2:2 and study note) They would think like the world, reflecting its desires, ambitions, prejudices, and hatreds. By contrasting the terms “friendship” and “enmity,” James powerfully warns his readers of the consequences of friendship with the world—they would make themselves enemies of God.

This expression and similar ones are frequently found in the Christian Greek Scriptures. The inspired writers used such phrases to introduce quotations from or references to parts of the Hebrew Scriptures. (Joh 19:37; Ro 4:3; 9:17; 10:11; Ga 4:30; 1Ti 5:18) The exact words that James here quotes are not found in any single scripture. But under inspiration, he paraphrases, or provides a summary of, basic ideas found in such scriptures as Ge 6:5; 8:21; Pr 21:10; Ec 9:3; and Ga 5:17. Other Bible writers similarly referred to general teachings found in some passages of the Hebrew Scriptures.—See, for example, 1Co 2:9 and study note; 2Ti 2:19 and study note.

In this context, “the spirit” seems to refer to the bad inclinations of sinful humans that move them to act wrongly in various ways. (See Glossary, “Spirit.”) Such a spirit has taken up residence within them because all humans are born imperfect. (Ge 8:21; Ro 7:18-20) Among the bad inclinations that humans inherit is a tendency to envy, which is rooted in selfishness. Such envious longing is not limited to a desire for material things; it could include a desire for prominence and power as well as similar selfish ambitions. (Ex 20:17; Nu 16:1-3; Ps 106:16, 17; Ec 4:4) If a Christian were to allow the world under Satan’s control to fill his heart with such desires, he would show in his attitude, speech, or conduct that he was “making himself an enemy of God.” (Jas 4:4) Many of the fights and conflicts that James mentioned in the preceding verses likely stemmed from certain Christians having an envious spirit.—Jas 4:1-3.

paragraphs.lemma: the undeserved kindness that He gives is greater
paragraphs.text: The undeserved kindness that God shows to imperfect humans is an expression of his generosity and abundant love. (See Glossary, “Undeserved kindness.”) God extends such kindness to humble ones who admit their sinful tendencies and ask for his help to overcome them. He gives such help by various means, such as his holy spirit, his inspired Word, and the support of faithful Christian brothers. (Lu 11:13; Heb 4:12; 10:25) God’s undeserved kindness, which he expresses in a wide variety of ways, is far greater, or more powerful, than inherited weaknesses, such as the tendency to envy. (Jas 4:5 and study note) Thus he helps Christians to conquer the weaknesses of their flesh and remain faithful.—Ro 7:24, 25.
To support the point he has just made regarding God’s undeserved kindness, James introduces a quote based on the Septuagint wording of Pr 3:34.—Compare Ps 138:6.

The Scriptures repeatedly condemn pride and haughtiness. (Ps 18:27; 101:5; Pr 16:18; Isa 2:17) Haughty people look down on their fellow man and arrogantly refuse either to search for God or to depend on him for guidance. (Ps 10:4) According to some reference works, the Greek term for “haughty” describes those who have an “exaggerated opinion of” themselves and who show this attitude “both toward God and toward men.” Jehovah opposes, or resists, those who harbor such a prideful attitude. The word here rendered “opposes” is a military term that conveys the idea of an army ready for battle. “The haughty ones” in effect make themselves enemies of God.—2Sa 22:28; Pr 6:16, 17; see study note on 1Pe 5:5.

In stark contrast to “the haughty ones,” humble people gladly acknowledge their reliance on their heavenly Father. They seek his help in order to conquer any weaknesses they may have, including the tendency to envy mentioned by James in the preceding verse. (Isa 66:2; Mt 18:3, 4; Jas 4:5) Jehovah shows his “undeserved kindness” by supplying such humble ones with his powerful holy spirit, which can help them to overcome any “fleshly desire.”—Ga 5:16.

James has just provided Christians with a powerful motive for being humble—they would receive God’s “undeserved kindness.” Here he follows up with practical instruction on what to do. (Jas 4:6) He noted earlier in his letter that “the wisdom from above is . . . ready to obey.” (Jas 3:17 and study note) Wise Christians gladly subject themselves to their loving, all-wise God by loyally obeying his commands. The verb “to subject oneself” is used in the Christian Greek Scriptures regarding young Jesus, who “continued subject” to the loving supervision of his parents. (Lu 2:51) Jesus also sets the perfect example of submission to his God and Father. (Joh 8:29; see 1Co 15:28 and study note.) Paul used the same Greek verb in his admonition that we “submit ourselves to the Father of our spiritual life.” (Heb 12:9) Those who loyally subject themselves to Jehovah as to a loving father also benefit from his protective care, as James goes on to show.—Ps 37:28; 68:5; 97:10.

Mere humans could never stand against, resist, or fight Satan, “the ruler of this world” and “the god of this system of things.” (Joh 12:31; 2Co 4:4) Yet, James assures Christians that they can oppose Satan and succeed by subjecting themselves to God and receiving his protection. (See study note on Therefore, subject yourselves to God in this verse; compare 1Pe 5:9.) Jehovah gives them a “complete suit of armor . . . to stand firm against the crafty acts of the Devil.” (Eph 6:11-13) Those who accepted God’s support would see the fulfillment of His promise that James records here: Satan and his demons would flee in defeat, having failed to corrupt a servant of God. Those wicked spirits flee, not in fear of the Christian, but in morbid dread of Christ and of Jehovah God.—Mt 8:28, 29; Jas 2:19 and study note; compare Mt 4:1-10.

This inspired invitation shows that Jehovah God wants to have a close personal relationship with his earthly children. (Compare Joh 4:23; Ac 17:26, 27.) When James wrote his letter, the concept of close friendship with Jehovah was not new. (Ps 25:14; 65:4; 73:28) Jehovah has always invited his people to draw close to him through prayer. (De 4:7; Ps 145:18) Jesus, by means of his example and his teachings, drew people even closer to his Father by offering them the clearest possible picture of Him. (Mt 11:27; Joh 1:18; 14:9; 15:15) Further, Christ’s sacrifice and his service as High Priest allow his followers to have their sins completely forgiven and to approach Jehovah freely. (Eph 1:7; Col 1:14; Heb 4:14-16) Jesus assured his followers that Jehovah wants to befriend them, that He has real affection for those who put faith in His Son. (Joh 16:27) The apostle Paul likewise taught Christians the vital goal of “drawing near to God,” which they could do by meditating on the hope He provides. (Heb 7:19) James’ readers could respond to the invitation to draw close to Jehovah by praying to him, by studying his Word, and by associating with his worshippers. (Jas 1:5, 6, 25; 5:13-16) Their every prayer, their every meditation on Jehovah and his Word, would help to strengthen that friendship. As they reflected appreciatively on Jehovah’s love and other qualities, their thinking would begin to harmonize with his thoughts, their heart would be purified, and they would be filled with a desire to please him as their dearest Friend.—Ps 19:14; 26:2; 86:11; 104:34; 139:23.

paragraphs.lemma: and he will draw close to you
paragraphs.text: James offers his readers the comforting assurance that humans who make the effort to draw close to Jehovah will be met with a positive, loving response. Jehovah promises to listen when such ones call on him, to guide and protect them, and to blot out their sins. (De 4:7; Ps 91:14; Ac 3:19) All, including those who have grown weak and have become involved in wrong practices, can turn to God and seek his help, confident that he will respond mercifully. (Compare Zec 1:3; Mal 3:7.) James’ wording in this verse does not imply that God cares about humans only after they take the initiative to draw close to him. From the very beginning, it was Jehovah who took the initiative to show love to all humans. (Ac 14:16, 17; 17:24, 26, 27; 1Jo 4:10, 19) When humans respond to that love, seeking God’s guidance, favor, and forgiveness, he draws even closer to them.—Compare Joh 6:44.

James does not direct this strong counsel and correction to every Christian. He has been addressing Christians who had grown weak in their faith, even likening them to “adulteresses” because they sought friendship with the world. (Jas 4:4 and study note) Many were giving in to their “fleshly desires,” which led them to engage in divisive fighting within the congregation. (Jas 4:1 and study note) Such expressions as “clean hands” or “innocent hands” were often used figuratively in the Hebrew Scriptures to represent righteous, pure conduct and actions. (Job 17:9; Ps 18:20, 24; 24:3, 4; 2Sa 22:21 and ftn.) Therefore, the counsel “cleanse your hands” meant that such sinners needed to change course and adjust their way of life in order to regain a clean standing with God and Christ.—Compare Isa 1:15, 16.

The expression “your hearts” refers to the inner person, including thoughts and motives. (See study note on 1Ti 1:5.) In order to purify his heart, an indecisive Christian needs to work hard at protecting his relationship with Jehovah. He needs to shield his own mind and heart by eliminating whatever might corrupt his thinking. (1Jo 3:3) If he purifies his heart in that way, he will be exclusively devoted to Jehovah. (1Ki 8:61 and ftn.; Ps 51:10; Jer 32:39; Mt 5:8 and study note) His hands, or good actions, will then be in harmony with his clean heart, or pure motives. The imagery of hands along with the heart is also used elsewhere in the Scriptures to refer to the inner person and his actions.—Job 31:7, 27; Ps 24:4; 58:2; 73:13; Pr 6:17, 18.

In referring to some Christians as “indecisive ones,” James uses a word that literally means “two-souled,” and it could also be rendered “double-minded.” (Compare 1Ki 18:21.) Such Christians were claiming to pursue friendship with God and Christ while clinging to the thinking and attitudes of the world.—Compare study note on Jas 1:8.

James addresses Christians who are sinning or who are indecisive and urges them to feel deep sorrow before God over their conduct and attitude. (See study notes on Jas 4:8.) One reference work explains that the Greek verb rendered “give way to misery” refers to “the inner sorrow” a person feels when he realizes how serious his sins are. (Compare Ro 7:24.) The next verbs, mourn and weep, refer to the outward expressions of that inner sorrow. (Mt 5:4 and study note; Mr 14:72) A person who feels “sadness in a godly way” gives evidence of sincere repentance.—2Co 7:10 and study notes.

paragraphs.lemma: Let your laughter be turned into mourning
paragraphs.text: James encourages his readers to change their attitude completely. (Compare Ec 7:3.) Those who do so will accept discipline and gain God’s favor.—Heb 12:11; compare Lu 18:13.

The Scriptures repeatedly condemn pride and arrogance, qualities that separate humans from one another and, more important, from God. (2Sa 22:28; Pr 6:16, 17; 1Pe 5:5) Therefore, James again reminds his readers of the need for humility if they are to “draw close to God.” (Jas 4:6-8) The Greek verb rendered “humble yourselves” has the basic meaning “to make [oneself] low.”—Compare Jas 1:10 and study note.

paragraphs.lemma: Humble yourselves in the eyes of Jehovah
paragraphs.text: Even righteous humans are sinful, and the sins they commit—including those that affect other humans—are in reality sins against God. (Compare Ps 51:4; Lu 15:21.) Those who recognize their sinfulness and their insignificance in comparison with God have strong reasons to cultivate humility, not just in relation to other humans but, more important, in relation to God. One reference work notes: “Humility is to know how lowly we really are before God.”
Or “in the sight of (before) Jehovah.”—Compare Lu 1:15 and study note; see also App. C3 introduction; Jas 4:10.

The Greek word here rendered “exalt” has the basic meaning of “lift up” and can be used figuratively to convey the idea of exalting or raising a person to a position of honor, dignity, and privilege. The context here could include the idea that God may exalt a repentant sinner by relieving him of feelings of guilt and by renewing his spirit. (Jas 4:6-9; compare Ps 51:10, 12, 13; Ac 3:19.) Both Jesus and the apostle Peter expressed the thought found in this verse—that God is pleased to exalt, or to show favor to, those who humble themselves before Him.—Mt 23:12; Lu 14:11; 18:14; 1Pe 5:6 and study notes.

paragraphs.lemma: Stop speaking against one another, brothers
paragraphs.text: The Greek term here rendered “speaking against” means “to speak ill of, speak degradingly of, speak evil of, defame, slander.” In this context, it refers to harsh, often malicious criticism of fellow believers. This Greek term was used in the Septuagint regarding the Israelites who spoke against Moses, who spoke against their brothers, and who slandered their neighbors. (Nu 12:8; Ps 50:20 [49:20, LXX]; 101:5 [100:5, LXX]) Those who speak against others often criticize those who are not present to defend themselves. In fact, Paul and Peter used forms of this Greek term to refer to backbiting and backbiters. (Ro 1:30; 2Co 12:20; 1Pe 2:1) Such critical individuals may have judged their fellow believers’ actions, motives, or manner of living, based on their own standards. They thus downgraded others, perhaps to prove themselves righteous or to exalt themselves.

paragraphs.lemma: speaks against law and judges law
paragraphs.text: James most likely refers, not to the Mosaic Law, but to God’s law in general. Earlier in his letter, he referred to “the royal law,” the law of love. (Jas 2:8 and study note; Mt 22:36-39 and study note; Ro 13:8-10) Christians who speak maliciously against or judge their fellow believers are at the same time speaking against and judging divine law. They are setting themselves above Jehovah’s law. (Compare Mr 7:1-13.) A Christian who judges a brother whom Jehovah does not judge is, in effect, implying that divine law is inadequate.—Compare Mt 7:1 and study note; Lu 6:37; Ro 2:1; 14:4.

paragraphs.lemma: There is only one who is Lawgiver and Judge
paragraphs.text: Christians who speak against their fellow believers make themselves lawgivers by setting their own standards of conduct for their fellow believers. They also take it upon themselves to pronounce harsh judgments on them. (See study note on Jas 4:11.) They fail to realize that the only rightful Lawgiver and Judge is Jehovah God. (Isa 33:22; 1Co 4:4 and study note) Only Jehovah has the ultimate authority to save and to destroy, that is, to grant the highest rewards and to inflict the severest punishments. (2Th 1:6-9; Jude 14, 15; see study note on Mt 10:28.) James’ pointed question “Who are you to be judging your neighbor?” shows how presumptuous it is to judge and condemn others.—Mt 7:1-5; Lu 6:37; see study note on Ro 14:4.
In Greek, this is an abrupt form of address. James uses it here and at Jas 5:1 as a kind of wake-up call to focus the attention of self-confident readers on the important admonition that follows.

The Greek word rendered “mist” might also mean “a mere puff of smoke.” With this vivid metaphor, James counters the faulty thinking he referred to in the preceding verse and stresses that life is brief and fragile. (Compare Job 14:1, 2; Ps 39:5; 102:11.) As one reference work puts it, the point is that human life is so short, so frail, that it could end at any time, “just as quickly as the morning sun dissipates the mist or as a shift in wind direction blows away smoke.”

James here emphasizes the need to take Jehovah’s will into account when doing or planning to do anything. James did not mean that Christians must always say this expression audibly; nor should they repeat it superstitiously or as an empty phrase. Instead, in whatever they do, they should try to discern God’s will and to act in harmony with it. (See study note on 1Co 4:19.) The apostle Paul often expressed the same idea, recognizing that any future plans he might make were subject to God’s will.—Ac 18:21; Ro 1:10; 15:32; Heb 6:3; for the use of the divine name in this verse, see App. C3 introduction; Jas 4:15.

paragraphs.lemma: you take pride in your arrogant boasting
paragraphs.text: In this context, James condemns those who boasted about what they would do in the future but who arrogantly failed to depend on God when making their plans. (Jas 4:13-15; compare Pr 27:1.) Instead of being ashamed of their boasting, they actually took pride in it. James tells these boasters frankly that all such boasting is wicked because it is based on false confidence in what they think they can achieve in the future.—Jer 9:23, 24.

paragraphs.lemma: it is a sin for him
paragraphs.text: James has just warned against boasting about material plans and accomplishments while failing to rely fully on Jehovah. (Jas 4:13-16) A Christian who understands this principle but fails to apply it commits a sin. However, James may have intended that these words apply in a broader sense to any sin of omission. Jesus himself plainly taught that a person could sin not only by deliberately committing a wrong but also by refusing to do what is right.—Mt 25:24-27; Lu 10:30-37; 12:47; 19:11-27; compare study note on Ro 3:9.
See study note on Jas 4:13.

Here James addresses wealthy people in general, much as Jesus did in his Sermon on the Mount. (Lu 6:24 and study note) Neither of them suggested that God disapproves of all men who are wealthy. However, many of the wealthy were driven by greed, oppressing the poor and underpaying workers. (Jas 5:4-6) Those who were inclined to trust in wealth instead of in God fell victim to “the deceptive power of riches.” (Mt 13:22) Jesus’ counsel to the rich helped his disciples to avoid that trap. (Lu 6:20 and study note) Following the same pattern, James’ words to the rich became a warning for all Christians. Those who pursued a materialistic course would ultimately “weep and wail” over losing not just possessions but, far worse, God’s favor and the hope of everlasting life.—Compare 1Ti 6:17-19.

In Bible times, a man’s wealth was measured not only in terms of his money—his gold and silver—but also in terms of the perishable goods that he possessed. Such goods might include livestock, grain, oil, wine, and clothing. (Ge 13:2; Job 1:3; Joe 2:19; Mt 11:8; Lu 12:16-19; see also Media Gallery, “The Clothing of the Rich and the Poor.”) All assets of that kind could perish, rot, or become spoiled. In this verse, James does more than emphasize how transitory such riches are; he also shows how worthless they can be if not used in the right way. He warns the rich that it is foolish to hoard earthly treasures and to trust in them. (Pr 11:28) Jesus made a similar point in his Sermon on the Mount, encouraging his followers to store up “treasures in heaven.” (Mt 6:19, 20) Here and in verse 3, James makes his point even more emphatic by describing events as if they had already taken place. He says “have rotted,” “has become,” and “have rusted away,” thus suggesting that the riches of such greedy people had already failed them.

paragraphs.lemma: Your gold and silver have rusted away
paragraphs.text: Throughout history, the wealthy have prized gold and silver because these metals are rare, durable, and beautiful and they do not rust or corrode as do more common metals, such as iron and copper. (Compare Isa 60:17.) James is using the expression “have rusted away” figuratively, possibly meaning that such riches “have become worthless” or “have decayed.” If rich men chose to hoard such material wealth and to trust in it, they would find that their possessions were as valueless as an iron object that had “rusted away” completely.—Pr 11:4; Zep 1:18.

paragraphs.lemma: and their rust will be a witness against you
paragraphs.text: James here warns the rich—including Christians who should have known better—to put their riches to good use rather than hoard them selfishly. The figurative “rust” of their “gold and silver” would “be a witness against” them, evidence that they had not used their possessions in an unselfish, generous way. (1Ti 6:17-19) They had failed to apply Jesus’ counsel to store up “treasures in heaven” and to “make friends for [themselves] by means of the unrighteous riches.”—Mt 6:19-21; Lu 16:9 and study notes.

paragraphs.lemma: What you have stored up will be like a fire in the last days
paragraphs.text: James here shows that those who kept hoarding their material possessions had stored up nothing of value. So they would have to answer to God for their selfishness and greed. If they failed to respond, they would face God’s righteous anger. Such anger will burn “like a fire in the last days” when God executes judgment against all ungodliness and unrighteousness.—Heb 10:26, 27; 2Pe 3:7; compare Ro 2:5.

paragraphs.lemma: The wages you have withheld . . . keep crying out
paragraphs.text: The Mosaic Law required that workers be paid at the end of each workday. (Le 19:13; De 24:14, 15; Mal 3:5) Here the unjustly withheld wages are personified—James describes those wages as “crying out” so that Jehovah God would notice the injustice and take action against those responsible for it. In a similar way, Jehovah described faithful Abel’s shed blood as “crying out” to Jehovah for justice. (Ge 4:9-11) James thus assures his readers that God sees all that is happening and will act in behalf of those whom the rich are defrauding.

paragraphs.lemma: have reached the ears of Jehovah of armies
paragraphs.text: James here emphasizes that Jehovah not only listens to “the cries for help” from oppressed workers but also responds by using his power in behalf of his servants. James reminds his readers that God has at his command vast armies of spirit creatures. (Ps 103:20, 21; 148:1, 2; Isa 1:24) The expression “Jehovah of armies” has its background in the Hebrew Scriptures, where it appears (with some variations) 283 times. In the Christian Greek Scriptures, it appears twice, here and at Ro 9:29. James is apparently alluding to Isa 5:9 according to the Septuagint, the only place where the Greek expression here rendered “the ears of Jehovah of armies” occurs in that translation. According to the wording in the Septuagint, the prophet shows that the unjust treatment of oppressed Israelites had “reached [or, “been heard in”] the ears of” Jehovah of armies.—See study notes on Ro 9:29; for the use of the divine name here at Jas 5:4, see App. C3; Jas 5:4.

Many rich ones fattened their figurative hearts by living solely for pleasure. (Lu 12:19; 21:34) Such overindulgence made them unresponsive and unfeeling toward God and insensitive to the needs of others. (Ps 119:70 and ftn.; Mt 13:15 and ftn.; Ac 28:27 and ftn.) By adding on the day of slaughter, James seems to create a word picture of animals that kept on gorging themselves even on the day when they were to be slaughtered. In a similar way, the wicked would continue to live for pleasure right up to the time when they would be judged adversely by God. (Lu 12:20) In the Hebrew Scriptures, a day of judgment is sometimes referred to as a day of slaughter.—Isa 34:2, 5-8; Jer 12:3.

Continuing to address “rich men,” James here rebukes wealthy opposers of Christianity who used the legal system to oppress and persecute not only Christ but also his innocent and righteous followers.—Jas 2:6; 5:1; Mt 27:1-3; Ac 4:27; see also Ac 6:8-14; 8:3.

paragraphs.lemma: you have murdered the righteous one
paragraphs.text: When James mentions “the righteous one” being murdered by “rich men,” he likely had in mind Jesus himself, since that expression is used to describe Jesus several times. (Jas 5:1; Ac 3:14, 15; 7:52; 22:14) Jesus was unjustly condemned to death by the Sanhedrin, which included a number of wealthy, influential men. (Mt 26:59, 66; compare study note on Joh 2:16.) In addition, when Saul of Tarsus was persecuting Jesus’ followers, Jesus told him: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Ac 9:4) Therefore, by extension, James may also have had in mind the condemnation and murder of Jesus’ righteous disciples.—Mt 24:9; Joh 16:2.

The idea of this rhetorical question seems to be that “the righteous one” mentioned in this verse, likely Jesus Christ, sees all the acts of oppression that James describes in this passage. As Jehovah’s righteous Judge, Jesus opposes those guilty of mistreating his faithful followers and will ultimately execute judgment on them.—Joh 5:22, 27; 2Th 1:7, 8; compare Ac 9:4.

James urges his oppressed fellow believers to “be patient” (or to “exercise patience,” as in verse 8) and wait on Jehovah. (See study note on Ga 5:22.) They needed to remain confident that Jehovah would bring about justice at the right time. (Lu 18:7) Christians who patiently endured “until the presence of the Lord” would be rewarded. Their oppressors would then be judged, and Christians would find real and lasting relief from all hardships and injustices.
That is, the invisible presence of the Lord Jesus Christ.—See Glossary, “Presence,” and study note on Mt 24:3.

A farmer had to work hard to plant and tend his crop, but he had no control over the weather or the growth of the plants. (Compare Mr 4:27, 28.) He needed to wait patiently for the harvest, trusting in Jehovah and the natural processes that He had put in place. (Isa 30:23; 55:10; Jer 5:24) The farmer could confidently expect that he would reap “the precious fruit of the earth” for himself and his family.

paragraphs.lemma: until the early rain and the late rain arrive
paragraphs.text: In Israel, “the early rain” came in the autumn (in October/November). It softened the soil that had been baked hard by the summer heat and allowed the farmer to plow his land in preparation for sowing. The much-anticipated “late rain” came in the spring (in March/April). It watered the growing crops so that they would ripen.—De 11:14; Jer 5:24; Joe 2:23; Zec 10:1; see App. B15.

James here urges his fellow believers to strengthen their figurative heart, or inner person. The expression “make . . . firm” translates a Greek verb that can convey the idea of gaining physical strength, for example, by eating something in preparation for a journey. (Compare Jg 19:5, 8 [and ftns.], where the same Greek expression is used in the Septuagint.) Here James uses this expression to refer to gaining inner strength—the kind of determination and courage that come from trusting in God. (Ps 112:7, 8) Christians who develop such firmness would be able to remain unwavering in faith, never giving way to doubt. (Col 1:23; 1Th 3:12, 13; Jas 1:6 and study note) They could gain this strength by meditating on their hope in the blessings to come at the time of “the presence of the Lord.”

paragraphs.lemma: the presence of the Lord has drawn close
paragraphs.text: James here urges his readers to keep “the presence of the Lord” Jesus Christ close in mind. (Compare 2Pe 3:11, 12 and study note.) Although none of those early Christians would live until that time, they needed to keep their hearts firm and their faith alive, trusting that the Lord’s presence would come at God’s appointed time. (Compare 2Th 2:1-3; see study note on verse 1.) Regardless of the timing, they needed to live their relatively short human lives as if the Lord’s presence were close at hand. (Ro 13:11) Doing so would help them to remain patient as well as to maintain their zeal for sharing the good news. But if they lost their patience and failed to endure, they would lose out on the blessings that God had in store for them.—Heb 10:36.

paragraphs.lemma: Do not grumble against one another
paragraphs.text: The Greek verb here rendered “grumble” can convey the idea of sighing or groaning inwardly. (Compare Heb 13:17, where it is rendered “sighing.”) So here James seems to focus on the feelings that Christians harbor toward one another, which could influence their speech and conduct. Thus, James warns his fellow believers to avoid complaining or murmuring about their spiritual brothers and sisters—even inwardly—since those who do such grumbling could bring judgment on themselves.—Mt 7:1, 2; Php 2:14 and study note.

This evidently refers to Christ Jesus. One reason for reaching this conclusion is that God “has entrusted all the judging” to him, starting with “the house of God.” (Joh 5:22; 1Pe 4:17) Also, James says that this Judge “is standing before the doors.” Similarly, at Mt 24:33, Jesus indicated that he would be “near at the doors” during the time of his presence. Then, during the great tribulation, he will judge “all the nations,” which are pictured as being composed of sheep and goats.—Mt 25:31, 32.

take as a pattern . . . the prophets: According to one lexicon, the Greek word here rendered “pattern” can refer to an example or model that “should spur one on to imitate it.” Jesus encouraged his disciples to imitate his way of doing things, saying: “I set the pattern for you.” (Joh 13:15) Similarly, James here urges his readers to imitate God’s faithful spokesmen from times past.—See Glossary, “Prophet.”

Such prophets as Elijah, Jeremiah, and Daniel set an example in suffering all kinds of adversities; they bravely faced opposition and risked death. (1Ki 19:9, 10; Jer 38:6; Da 6:16, 17; Heb 11:36-38) Some were beaten, imprisoned, or even murdered by those who did not want to hear the word of God. (1Ki 18:4, 13; 22:7, 8, 19-28; 2Ch 16:7-10; 24:20-22) Both Jesus and Stephen referred to the bitter persecution endured by the prophets. (Mt 23:31, 32 and study note; Ac 7:52) Despite those trials, the prophets were exemplary in the exercising of patience—they waited on Jehovah and completely relied on him.—2Ch 36:15, 16; Jer 20:8-11; Mic 7:7, ftn.

paragraphs.lemma: who spoke in the name of Jehovah
paragraphs.text: The main objective of Jehovah’s faithful prophets was to convey what God wanted people to hear. They spoke “in the name of Jehovah,” representing him. Thus, they often used such expressions as “this is what Jehovah says” (2Sa 7:5; Isa 56:1; Jer 2:2; Am 1:6; Ex 5:1; Eze 2:4; Zec 1:3), “hear the word of Jehovah” (Eze 37:4; Hos 4:1), and “hear . . . what Jehovah is saying” (Mic 6:1).—For the use of the divine name in this verse, see App. C3 introduction; Jas 5:10.

Christians who have patiently endured suffering can be considered happy, or blessed, because Jehovah favors them and approves of them. (Mt 5:10-12; Jas 1:2-4; see study note on Mt 5:3.) Jehovah will reward all those who endure faithfully, as he rewarded Job, whom James mentions in this verse.

Job is an outstanding example of what true endurance means for a servant of Jehovah. (Jas 1:4 and study note) Satan robbed Job of his servants, his ten children, his health, and his wealth. Even worse, Satan deceived Job into thinking that Jehovah was the one attacking him. Then Job was plagued by false comforters who tried to convince him that he was wicked and that his integrity did not matter to God. Yet, Job endured, steadfastly refusing to give up his integrity.—Job 1:13-21; 2:6-10; 7:20; 22:2, 3; 25:4-6; 27:5.

This is the only place where Job’s name appears in the Christian Greek Scriptures. James mentions him after discussing God’s prophets who had suffered evil. (Jas 5:10) Unlike such men as Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Jonah, Job is not specifically identified as a prophet. (Mt 2:17; 3:3; 12:39) However, Job did at times act as a spokesman for God. (See Glossary, “Prophet.”) For example, he spoke correctly about things that he could have known only with the help of God’s spirit. (Job 14:13-15; 26:7) Additionally, Job offered sacrifices in behalf of others, as did other faithful patriarchs who served as God’s prophets, such as Noah and Abraham.—Ge 8:20; 9:24-27; 12:7; 20:7; 1Ch 16:16, 17, 21-23.

James here refers to the loving way in which Jehovah not only brought an end to the trials Satan had inflicted on Job but also showered him with many blessings. He restored Job’s health and reputation and even doubled his former wealth. Job and his wife were blessed with ten more children. And Jehovah exonerated Job from all the vicious slander that his false accusers had heaped on him. Jehovah also blessed Job with deep insight into His wisdom, majesty, and power. Further, Job’s tender and affectionate God granted him another 140 years of life as a reward for his faithful endurance.—Job 42:1-6, 16, 17.
For the use of the divine name, see App. C3 introduction; Jas 5:11.
For the use of the divine name, see App. C3 introduction; Jas 5:11.

This expression renders a single Greek word that might also be translated “very compassionate.” According to one lexicon, this Greek word means “with empathy in one’s very inner being.” Another lexicon says, “full of pity, very kind.” The Hebrew Scriptures clearly teach that Jehovah has profound compassion for his faithful servants, and he shows them mercy. (Compare Ex 34:6; Ne 9:17; Ps 103:8; 112:4; Isa 63:9; Joe 2:13.) However, in ancient times, such a concept was quite foreign to many. For instance, some Greek philosophers taught that pity was a weakness and that no god would allow such an emotion to disturb his serenity. Jesus helped to show how wrong such notions were. He perfectly reflected his Father, Jehovah, so he was often “moved with pity” over the suffering of others.—Lu 7:13; Mt 9:36 and study note; Mr 6:34; compare study notes on Joh 11:33, 35.
James adds that Jehovah is also “merciful,” meaning that God’s deep feelings of compassion move him to act, to help people in need.—Lu 6:36; compare study note on 2Co 1:3.

paragraphs.lemma: Above all, my brothers, stop swearing
paragraphs.text: This admonition echoes what Jesus said about swearing, or oath-taking. Neither Jesus nor James meant that all oath-taking is wrong. Rather, disciples of Christ, who consistently speak the truth, do not need to strengthen their every statement or promise with an oath. (Mt 5:34 and study note; Eph 4:15, 25) James’ readers also needed to avoid the view held by some Jews that a person who swore “by heaven” or “by earth” could retract his oath later. (Mt 5:34 and study note, 35) By prefacing his exhortation to “stop swearing” with the expression “above all,” James emphasizes that his readers should give special attention to this matter.—See also Mt 5:37 and study note.

paragraphs.lemma: Is there anyone suffering hardship among you?
paragraphs.text: The Greek term here rendered “suffering hardship” is broad in meaning and may refer to any kind of suffering, including hardship because of sickness, economic problems, and disappointment, as well as persecution. Earlier in his letter, James mentions hardships that befall true worshippers because they serve God. (Jas 1:2, 12; 2:6, 7; 5:4) Additionally, he cites the examples of the hardships endured by the prophets and Job. (Jas 5:10, 11) James advises all those suffering such hardships to pray for help to continue faithful.—Compare Ro 12:12.

James here encourages any Christian who is “suffering hardship” to make it a practice, or habit, to turn to God in prayer. Jesus was a man of prayer throughout his earthly life. For example, he prayed when he had serious decisions to make and when he underwent trials. (Lu 5:16 and study note; 6:12, 13; 22:41; Heb 5:7 and study notes) He often encouraged his followers to pray. (Lu 22:40 and study note) In a similar way, the apostle Paul encouraged Christians to “persevere in prayer” and to pray regarding “everything” that could make them anxious or affect their relationship with God. (Ro 12:12; Php 4:6 and study note) Thus, Christians should “keep asking God” for wisdom and leave their problems in his hands.—Jas 1:5; compare 1Pe 5:7.

paragraphs.lemma: Is there anyone in good spirits?
paragraphs.text: The Greek word for “be in good spirits” can mean to “be cheerful,” and some translations render it that way. The word describes an attitude that does not necessarily depend on outward circumstances. (Compare Ac 27:22, 25, where the same word is rendered “take courage.”) By mentioning both those “suffering hardship” and those who were “in good spirits,” James shows that a Christian always has good reasons to think about God and turn to Him in prayer.

Or “sing praises to God.” James encourages Christians who are “in good spirits” to express their joy by singing songs of praise to Jehovah.—Mt 26:30 and study note; Eph 5:19 and study notes; see Glossary, “Psalm.”

paragraphs.lemma: Is there anyone sick among you?
paragraphs.text: This question could also be rendered “Is there anyone feeling weak among you?” The Greek verb used in this phrase is often rendered “be sick” when the context specifically refers to physical illness. (Joh 11:2; Ac 9:37; Php 2:27) However, in other contexts, the term is broader in meaning and is often translated “to be weak.” (Ac 20:35; 1Co 8:11, 12; 2Co 11:29; 12:10; related forms of the word are rendered “weak” at 1Th 5:14 and “weakness(es)” at 2Co 12:9, 10.) It is noteworthy that James advises those who are sick, or weak, to “call the elders” rather than a physician. Thus, James does not seem to be referring primarily to a physical illness. (Jas 5:15, 16, 19, 20) Jesus stated that those who were physically ill would “need a physician.” (Mt 9:12) Of course, challenging circumstances, including physical illness, often leave Christians emotionally and physically exhausted, depressed, and in need of encouragement from the elders. (2Co 12:7b-10; see study note on verse 7.) The Greek word found at Jas 5:14 is also used of those who have “weaknesses in [their] faith,” perhaps requiring assistance to resolve certain doubts. (Ro 14:1, 2) In the next verse, James indicates that some weak ones may have “committed sins.” In that case, the elders could help them to restore their relationship with God.—Ga 6:1 and study notes; Jude 22, 23.

James here urges one who has become weakened emotionally or spiritually to request assistance from the elders in the Christian congregation. (See Glossary, “Elder; Older man.”) As the apostle Paul had indicated, elders should be ready and willing to assist such fellow believers. (Ac 20:35; 1Th 5:14) If a person’s weakness involved sinful conduct, the elders would be ready to help the erring one to restore his relationship with God.—Jas 5:15.

James here urges elders to pray with and for those who are feeling weak, are discouraged, or are struggling spiritually. (See study note on Is there anyone sick among you? in this verse.) A Christian dealing with any of those situations would likely feel comforted when sensing the elders’ genuine concern and compassion as they earnestly prayed to Jehovah in his behalf. He could demonstrate his own faith and express his agreement with the prayer by saying a heartfelt “amen.”—Compare Ne 8:6.

Here James refers to the soothing and healing properties of olive oil to illustrate how elders can help their fellow Christians. (Isa 1:6; Lu 10:34 and study note) Such loving shepherds use thoughts from God’s Word to encourage and comfort those who have been weakened by trials, emotional exhaustion, or discouragement. The weakened one could find refreshment in such a discussion. For one who had committed sins, the loving efforts of the elders could help him to restore and strengthen his relationship with Jehovah.—Ps 141:5.

With this phrase, James emphasizes that when the elders apply spiritual oil, offering Scriptural help, they do not lean on their own ideas; rather, they seek to reflect Jehovah’s mind on matters. In doing so, they recognize Jehovah’s authority and humbly acknowledge that they themselves are not the source of comfort and spiritual healing. Such blessings originate with Jehovah.—2Co 1:3, 4; for the use of the divine name here, see App. C3 introduction; Jas 5:14.

This phrase refers to a sincere, heartfelt prayer offered by congregation elders in behalf of a fellow worshipper who has requested their help. In such a prayer, the elders might ask Jehovah to raise the individual up by granting the emotional and spiritual strength needed to recover from a weakened condition. They pray with full confidence, trusting that Jehovah hears and answers such petitions. (Ps 65:2; Jas 1:5, 6; 1Jo 5:14) According to one reference work, the Greek word translated “prayer,” as used here, conveys the idea of “a fervent wish or strong petition,” much like a heartfelt supplication.

The Greek word used here (kaʹmno, which differs from the word rendered “is . . . sick” in the preceding verse) could also be translated “the tired one.” (Compare Heb 12:3, where a form of the word is rendered “get tired.”) A faithful Christian might become emotionally or spiritually exhausted because of distressing circumstances, oppression, or injustice. (Ec 7:7; Isa 32:2; 2Co 12:7-10) Whether a servant of God is suffering from physical or emotional exhaustion or from spiritual weakness, the prayers of caring elders will make him well, that is, will strengthen him and assist him in his recovery.

Jehovah is eager to offer loving support to a Christian who has become weakened, helping him regain emotional and spiritual strength. (Isa 41:10) God does so by reassuring the tired one of His love and gently helping him overcome discouraging thoughts—such as the mistaken belief that God has abandoned him. (Heb 13:5) Jehovah promises that even those who feel completely exhausted can find renewed strength and hope by turning to him for help.—Isa 40:30, 31; Php 4:13; Col 1:11; 1Pe 5:10; for the use of the divine name in this verse, see App. C3 introduction; Jas 5:15.

paragraphs.lemma: Also, if he has committed sins, he will be forgiven
paragraphs.text: See study note on Jas 5:14.

paragraphs.lemma: Therefore, openly confess your sins to one another
paragraphs.text: It seems that James here continues his discussion regarding someone who “has committed sins,” as mentioned in the preceding verse. (Jas 5:15) When a Christian confesses a serious sin to “the elders of the congregation,” he demonstrates his sincere repentance; by making such a confession, he would be taking an important step toward restoring his relationship with Jehovah. (Jas 5:14; compare Isa 57:17-19; Jer 33:6, 7.) He would be following the examples of God’s faithful servants from ancient times who humbly recognized their sinful condition. (Nu 21:7; Ps 51:4) When they confessed their sins to God—and in some cases to fellow humans—they showed that they were aware of their wrongdoing and were genuinely repentant. (Ne 1:6; Ps 32:5; Da 9:20; compare Mr 1:5.) For Christians, not every sin called for them to confess to the congregation elders. However, Christians could still apply the principle of confessing sins “to one another” by acknowledging a mistake or wrongdoing that affected a fellow believer. Humbly doing so might be the first step in restoring or improving their relationships with one another.—Mt 5:23, 24 and study notes.

James had already instructed “the elders of the congregation” to pray over fellow Christians who had become weakened because of trials, discouragement, or even their own sinfulness. (Jas 5:14, 15) Now he encourages all to “pray for one another.” As used in this verse, the Greek verbs for “confess” and “pray” suggest continuous action. So the whole phrase could also be rendered: “Make it your habit to confess your sins to one another and to pray for one another.” (See study note on Therefore, openly confess your sins to one another in this verse.) Jehovah is pleased to see his people showing their mutual love and concern by praying for one another.—See study note on 2Co 1:11.

paragraphs.lemma: A righteous man’s supplication has a powerful effect
paragraphs.text: James here encourages the congregation to pray in behalf of fellow Christians because such supplication, or earnest prayer, “has a powerful effect” (lit., “has much force when it is at work”). (See study notes on Ac 4:31; Php 4:6.) Jehovah is always pleased to answer requests that are offered “according to his will.” (1Jo 5:14, 15) James notes that the one offering the prayer must be righteous in God’s eyes, one who exercises faith in Jehovah and seeks to please Him. Next, James illustrates this point by mentioning Elijah’s prayers of faith. (Jas 5:17, 18) In some cases, a supplication may make a difference in what God does and when he does it.—Isa 38:1-6; 2Co 1:8-11 and study notes on verses 8 and 11; Phm 22 and study note.

James’ Jewish readers especially held Elijah in high regard. They knew that he was a great prophet and a bold, righteous man of prayer. (1Ki 17:20-22; 18:24, 36, 37) They also knew that his name was even applied to the forerunner of the Messiah. (Mal 4:5; Mt 11:13, 14) Though people thought of Elijah as such an outstanding man, he was not without weakness or frailty, as James goes on to show.

paragraphs.lemma: a man with feelings like ours
paragraphs.text: The Greek word here rendered “with feelings like” is defined as “experiencing similarity in feelings or circumstances.” It is translated “having the same infirmities as” at Ac 14:15. Faithful Elijah once felt so dispirited that he said he was no better than his forefathers, who were mere dust and bones in the grave, unable to do anything for anyone. He poured out those intense feelings to God, even asking to die. He later revealed that he thought that his work had been in vain and that he felt alone and frightened. (1Ki 19:1-4, 9, 10) James clearly does not portray Elijah as superhuman or unique. Rather, in saying “with feelings like ours,” James acknowledges that much the same could be said about any ordinary human servant of Jehovah, including himself and his readers. (Ro 3:23; 5:12; Jas 5:10-13) Yet, Elijah’s heartfelt prayers led to extraordinary results.

Under inspiration, James mentions a detail not found in the Hebrew Scriptures account about Elijah—that the prophet prayed for it “not to rain” and that Jehovah brought the drought in response to that prayer. (1Ki 17:1) The Greek expression rendered “prayed earnestly” literally reads, “prayed with prayer.” That wording reflects a Hebrew way of expressing intensity. In the next verse, James reveals that Elijah “prayed again,” this time for the drought to end. (Jas 5:18) The account in the Hebrew Scriptures does not explicitly mention this prayer either, but it does describe Elijah’s posture on Mount Carmel—he bowed low to the earth, a position often associated with prayer. This posture also suggests great humility and intensity of feelings.—1Ki 18:42, 43; compare Ge 24:26; Mt 26:39.

paragraphs.lemma: for three years and six months
paragraphs.text: See study note on Lu 4:25.

if anyone . . . is led astray from the truth: A Christian could be led off course or wander from the truth as a result of tests of faith, false teachings, or his own desires. (Lu 8:13; 2Th 2:3; 2Ti 3:6; Heb 13:9) Such straying could happen gradually. (Compare Heb 2:1 and study note.) The Greek verb here rendered “is led astray” also occurs at Mt 18:12, 13, where it describes a sheep that has strayed from the flock. Jesus indicated that a loving shepherd would make every effort to find that sheep. A person who has strayed from the truth would be in danger of damaging his relationship with Jehovah and ultimately losing out on everlasting life. So James encourages all Christians, especially shepherds in the congregation, to try to bring back anyone who has been “led astray” from the path of truth.

The Greek word here rendered “turns . . . back” can convey the idea of redirecting a person, helping him to change his way of thinking and to return to God. (See study note on Ac 3:19.) To motivate a sinner to repent and return to doing what is right, a Christian must be patient and persistent. (Compare 2Pe 3:9.) Thus he may help to save him [the sinner] from death, that is, from losing out on everlasting life. In any case, such efforts please Jehovah.—Eze 34:16; Mt 18:14; Jude 22, 23.

paragraphs.lemma: will cover a multitude of sins
paragraphs.text: In the Scriptures, the expression “to cover sin” is often used to emphasize Jehovah’s willingness to forgive sin. (Ps 32:1; 85:2, ftn.; Ro 4:7 and study note) God responds to sincere repentance by forgiving even serious sins. The phrase “a multitude of sins” focuses, not on the number of sins or the degree of wickedness involved, but on the vast extent of Jehovah’s forgiveness. (Compare Lu 7:47.) His undeserved kindness is far greater than any sin. (Ps 103:3; Eph 2:4, 5; Col 2:13) A Christian who helps his erring brother to grasp the wrongfulness of his course and to seek divine forgiveness acts as an instrument in Jehovah’s hands.—Ga 6:1; 1Ti 4:16.
